subtopic: CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, by providing a veritable framework for this country's economic, intellectual and cultural pursuits, our national telecommunications and broadcasting system is undoubtedly one of the strongest ties that bind Canadians together.
This system, which is unequalled in the whole world, is one of our most brilliant achievements and embodies the prophetic vision of men like Sir John A. Macdonald and R. B. Bennett. It is also the result of active co-operation between the private and public sectors, which together have taken advantage of new technologies and have harmonized their efforts with those of our regulatory agencies.
The Bill to amend the Canadian Radio-Television and Telecommunications Commission Act, Bill C-20, marks an important phase in the development of telecommunications in Canada. The purpose of this Bill is, basically, to clarify and regulate the sharing of powers and to seek a proper balance between the Government's objectives and those of the regulatory agency and our telecommunications system.
Before going into the details of this Bill, I would like to touch briefly on the history and present situation of telecommunications, legislation and regulatory measures in this country.
Canada's broadcasting policy has been evolving ever since the first radio broadcast in 1919. In the twenties, radio broadcasting was developing so fast that there was utter confusion on the airwaves, and it became clear that a set of regulations would be needed. In 1928, the first Canadian Royal Commission on Radio Broadcasting was formed.
The Royal Commission, chaired by Sir John Aird, recommended setting up a national broadcasting system. A report was submitted in 1929 under the Liberal Prime Minister Mackenzie King, who was unable to act on the recommendations before the end of his term. It was therefore up to the Progressive Conservative Government under Prime Minister Bennett to act, which it did by tabling the first Canadian legislation on radio broadcasting in the House of Commons.
Here is what the Prime Minister said when he tabled the broadcasting Bill:

CRTC Act
This country must have absolute control over Canadian broadcasting, without interference or influence from foreigners. Without such control, broadcasting cannot be the vehicle to convey national aspirations and unity. Only state ownership of the system will guarantee the people of this country, without reference to class or locality, equal benefits from broadacsting.
He went on to say:
It may be that in the future, when science is even further adanced, it will be desirable to make other arrangements.
It was therefore the Progressive Conservative Government of R.B. Bennett which established the predecessor of the CBC, then the Canadian Broadcasting Commission.
When the Conservatives took office in 1957, they came to the conclusion that the Broadcasting Act, dating back to the former Bennett Conservative administration, was already 22 years old and no longer met current needs. The private sector had expanded considerably and was anxious to play a larger role in the growing broadcasting system. The public sector, acting as both regulatory agency and broadcaster, was in a position to regulate its own competitors. Such blatant conflicts of interests could not be perpetuated.
The Diefenbaker Government therefore took steps to steer a new course in the broadcasting field. It introduced a piece a legislation which, for the first time, made a clear-cut distinction between regulatory and broadcasting operations. It established the Board of Broadcast Governors, which was eventually replaced by today's Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission, the CRTC.
As to the CRTC, it was set up in two stages: First, the Canadian Radio-television Commission was created by Parliament in 1968 under the Broadcasting Act, replacing the Board of Broadcast Governors. Second, the responsibility for regulating telecommunications was transferred from the Canadian Transport Commission to the Canadian Radio-television Commission in 1976, under the Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission Act.
The Commission's major responsibility is to regulate and supervise all aspects of the Canadian broadcasting system for the purpose of implementing the broadcasting policy stated in Section 3 of the Act. Section 3 states, among other things, and I quote:
-the objectives of the broadcasting policy for Canada ... can best be achieved by providing for the regulation and supervision of the Canadian broadcasting system by a single independent public authority.
Following the Second World War, the technology of telecommunication has undergone constant and important changes in all aspects. By reason more especially of recent achievements in computer technology, digitalization and interconnection have brought far-reaching changes in our telephone networks, at a time when the telephone, telegraph and computer industries were opening up to competition. Technological progress has been such that the traditional differences between
those services have been virtually overshadowed. In the meantime, Canadians, foreseeing the new prospects of novel technologies have been requesting increased services, at affordable prices, of course.
If the array of new computer technologies can on the one hand help us reach our goals with respect to telecommunications, whether for the assertion of our Canadian identity and cultural traits, for this country's unification, for a greater opening to the world, or for achieving closer links with our remote communities, it does on the other hand present legislators and regulating agencies, among others, with a major challenge, because this is actually the responsibility of the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission.
Our legislative and regulatory mechanism, the essential part of which was implemented more than 17 years ago, could not foresee the current technological upheavals. Clearly it is outdated as to the cultural, economic and social potential of high technologies. If it is not to become a barrier against economic growth, technological innovation, and cultural development, we must at all costs bring it in line with today's realities, whether it is deregulation in the United States and its impact on Canada, or the spectacular developments in satellite services. In the area of telecommunications and broadcasting, the time for a change has come.
As my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), stated in his economic statement last November 8, and I quote:
There is a clear need for a national telecommunications policy to take advantage of the opportunities presented by rapidly advancing technology and the growing demand by Canadians for new telecommunications services.
Why is this? Because, as the Minister of Finance explained, the telecommunications sector, perhaps more than any other in Canada at the present time, offers opportunities for important market-driven innovation, if governments' regulatory interventions are kept to an essential minimum. Through regulatory reform, government can spur innovation and provide a major stimulus to the Canadian economy.
Indeed, for us deregulation will not mean unfair competition, because we firmly intend to proceed gradually and responsibly. Is telephony not in fact a field where competition is now proving its usefulness? Since the 50's, Canadians have enjoyed the benefits of competitive development by CN-CP Telecommunications and telephone companies of ultrahigh frequency facilities.
As far as terminals are concerned, consumers and businesses have had the option since 1980 to choose to purchase their equipment from a great number of suppliers or to rent it from their local telephone company. For subscribers, this competition means a much greater choice of sets, lower prices and a multitude of new ideas in phone design. As for switched services, CNCP Telecommunications obtained the right in
January 31, 1985

1979 to set up an interconnection with Bell telephone system, thus allowing them to provide this type of service as well for data transmission for instance. In 1981, this interconnection right was extended to British Columbia Telephone. The CRTC has just concluded a series of public hearings and is considering a request of CNCP for an interconnection with Bell and BC Telephone to provide long distance telephone services to the public. Faced with these increasing pressures and to allow more competition in a sector which has traditionally been very strictly regulated, the government has undertaken to review its telecommunications policy in 1985 and is now looking at the state of competition in this field.
Another example of a regulated sector is that of satellite signals. Since 1983, individuals no longer require a radio permit to use a dish antenna to receive programs which are not retransmitted. Provided they do not redistribute the signals, taverns and hotel bars can also use a dish antenna without applying for a radio or television broadcasting permit.
On December 20, 1984, I announced a revamping of the regulatory policy for satellite signals to benefit small television broadcasting systems and help badly served communities to gain access to a greater variety of programs. In addition to helping the television broadcasting industry and interested consumers, this initiative will make the Canadian television broadcasting system more flexible and stronger.
As for our commitment to continue to regulate where necessary, a good example of this can be found in the measures I will introduce to provide the CRTC with the necessary power to control abusive programming. I shall speak further on this question in a few moments.
There will be two underlying guidelines to our telecommunications policy:
First, everyone involved will automatically be consulted. In doing so, we shall certainly be breaking ground with regard to the development of our country's telecommunications policy. These consultations are necessary because, to paraphrase Montesquieu, "the intent of laws depends on whether you live before or beyond the mountains".
[DOT] (U20)
Secondly, in all cases where deregulation will not be prejudicial to the interests of Canadian consumers, we will deregulate.
The bill which we have submitted for your consideration is therefore the first stage of a basic review of the legislative and regulatory framework of our telecommunications system. Its passage is of the highest importance if the government is to have the powers it needs to make our regulations more flexible or even repeal them in the case of services that can be left open to free competition although some form of regulated competition could also be considered. The bill is in effect a general framework which will allow us to implement the necessary
CRTC Act
reforms and carry out the reshaping of our telecommunication policy.
Let us consider now the main provisions of the bill.
Part I of the bill amends the CRTC Act to enable the Governor in Council to give binding policy directions. Those directions would be laid before Parliament and it would have the opportunity to take them under advisement before they are formally put into effect.
Although the 1968 legislation setting up the CRTC did not generally grant that power to the government, I think it is necessary today to specify that the government and not the CRTC should develop the broadcasting and telecommunication policies. That position is supported by the provinces, the industry and the Commission itself. Moreover, it was ratified by the Lambert Commission and one of its specific recommendations was as follows:
The constituent acts of Independent Deciding and Advisory Bodies contain provisions allowing for policy directives from the Governor in Council.
This principle was also supported in 1980 by a special parliamentary committee of the House of Commons on Regulatory Reform as follows:
-that Cabinet can issue binding policy directives ... to the Canadian Radiotelevision and Telecommunications Commission.
The relation between the government and the Commission has been under review for many years. If there is an aspect that the review and public debate have brought out, it is that the government should be responsible for the drawing up of policy and that the CRTC should be in charge of its implementation within the legislative framework set up by Parliament. The division of powers between the government and the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission reflects the democratic principle that the government alone is entitled to develop the main policies of the country because of its accountability to the electorate through Parliament.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
The government having the power to give formal directions to the CRTC, will implement its policy in the telecommunication and broadcasting areas. If it did not have that power, it could have no influence on the development of policy and consequently could not be called to account. As in the present legislation, it could only react after the fact and ask for reconsideration of specific decisions made by the CRTC.
But, as Cardinal de Richelieu so aptly said, and I quote:
Thus, Ministers of State must often remind themselves that it is more important to consider the future than the present, and that it is easier to anticipate problems than after one is faced with them.
I strongly believe that by making the government accountable for the policy to Parliament, we will eliminate a number of ambiguities such as the parabolic antennas, ambiguities

January 31, 1985
CRTC Act
which create major obstacles to the dynamic development of this industry.
In my opinion, the government must implement measures designed to encourage and help Canadians to take risks and compete in making telecommunications equipment, producing television programs and developing the many products that will be required by the new communication environment. The responsibility of the government to provide such a favourable framework goes hand in hand with its accountability to Parliament.
Part I of this bill also adds to the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission Act Subsection 14.6, which enables the Governor in Council to direct the Commission to deregulate the telecommunication services which can be provided on a competitive basis. Invested with this authority, the government will be able to decide whether it is in the public interest not to regulate a number of telecommunications services within a monopolistic structure because of the competitive character of the market. I have in mind for instance the cellular mobile radio telephones. The nature of this technology is such that these services could be provided by competitive organizations. It would be therefore illogical to regulate, under monopolistic principles, services such as these which allow for a more competitive system.
Part I provides also that the Governor in Council may order a deregulation if he is of the opinion that a service is subject to a degree of competition sufficient to ensure just and reasonable tolls, rates or charges.
Mr. Speaker, I could not overemphasize the fact that, in our mind, the deregulation powers should always be used with a good measure of judgment. The government would have first to convince itself that such a measure is justified before ordering the CRTC to implement it.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to indicate to all Hon. Members that while introducing a power to give instructions and a power to order deregulation, the government remains aware of the need to prevent any abuse. I should like to remind them that this bill contains four safeguards in this end: First, under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, the Government will not be able to issue directions limiting freedom of speech; second, the Bill specifically prohibits the Government from issuing directions in respect of the issuance of a broadcasting licence to a particular person or the amendment or renewal of a licence; third, the Minister of Communications shall consult with the CRTC before directions are issued by the Government to the Commission; fourth, to allow for parliamentary and public consideration of the directions, it is provided that such directions must be laid before Parliament and referred to the appropriate committee, and that they will not become effective until thirty days after Parliament was notified thereof. This measure will enable Parliament and the Canadian
public to consider carefully all directions before they are implemented.
Parliament has a major role to play in ensuring that the Government accounts for its policies and facilitates the public's participating in the debate. I think parliamentary committees are the key to the Government's accountability. Committees can summon witnesses, including Ministers of the Crown, and ask for any clarification, explanations and guarantees deemed necessary. They provide an excellent forum for Canadians who wish to make their views on official policy known to their representatives. I am convinced that the guarantees provided by the Bill and applying to the power to issue directions and the power to order deregulation ensure the Government will remain accountable and promote healthy and active involvement by all Canadians.
Part II of the Bill provides for a new policy objective that will become part of Section 3 of the Broadcasting Act. This objective concerns programming of an abusive nature, and its purpose is to define the CRTC's responsibility in this respect. It will be an incentive to broadcasters to be increasingly aware of the problem, and here is the wording:
"(c. 1) the programming provided by the Canadian broadcasting system should respect and promote the equality and dignity of all individuals, groups or classes of individuals regardless of race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex, age or mental or physical disability;"
I should think it is imperative to pass legislation to make absolutely sure that there is no room for abusive programs within the Canadian broadcasting system. The Speech from the Throne reaffirmed the Government's commitment to ensure that social justice in Canada would progress at the same pace as the needs of Canadians. It did contain an announcement concerning this measure which is aimed at eliminating those abusive programs.
In its June 1984 report, the parliamentary sub-committee on sexually abusive broadcasting recommended that we add to Broadcasting Act Section 3 a provision stating that programs must advocate the right of women to equality. I might point out that, besides guaranteeing the equality and dignity of women, this legislation is aimed at preventing all forms of vexations with respect to racial, national or ethnic origin, or else colour, religion, age or mental or physical disability.
Parts II and III of the Bill contain other amendments to the Broadcasting Act and the Radio Act whose purpose is to clarify and simplify the regulatory process. Since in some cases the legislative provisions of those two Acts are definitely outdated, they must be amended to take recent progress into account.
For instance, in the Lount case involving Winnipeg's Holiday Inn, the Federal Court ruled that the current wording of the Broadcasting Act and the Radio Act was deficient and must be amended so as to define the status of those systems
January 31, 1985

which redistribute satellite signals, particularly in the case of hotels and high-rise buildings. Clauses 2 and 7 of this Bill are intended to alleviate that anomaly. They are very technical precisely because they will eliminate that kind of discrepancy in the legislation.
Clause 2, for instance, which amends the Broadcasting Act, provides that any person who transmits or distributes by means of telecommunication, otherwise than solely as a telecommunication common carrier or whether or not for any consideration, any programming received by radiocommunication is deemed to be carrying on a broadcasting undertaking. This means that individuals who redistribute satellite signals will be subjected to the Broadcasting Act. Similarly, Clause 7 brings consequential changes to the Radio Act in compliance with this amendment to the Broadcasting Act. Under such provisions, the Government and the CRTC would be empowered to implement the satellite signals policy which I announced on December 20, 1984.
Part II of this Bill also provides amendments to the Broadcasting Act to eliminate factors preventing the regulatory system from being more effective and cost-efficient. To that end, it is proposed in Clause 5, and I quote:
First, to extend from five to seven years the maximum term of a broadcasting licence. This will give broadcasters an incentive to improve on their performance, in return for longer licence terms, and this will help reduce the regulatory burden.
Second, to increase the CRTC's power to exempt people from the requirement that they hold broadcasting licences. This will reduce the regulatory burden imposed by the Commission in cases where it is neither useful nor necessary to issue licences.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would like to recall the major challenge put forth by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in his economic statement. He more or less invited us to redefine the Goverment's role which should be first and foremost to bring about a climate favourable to our growth which alone will enable us to create jobs, promote innovation and get ready to face the changes to come.
The legislation now being considered moves us in that direction by giving the Government the power to instruct the CRTC to order the deregulation of certain services if necessary. This Bill will stimulate and energize the telecommunications and broadcasting sector for the benefit of Canadians everywhere. No doubt also that broadcasters and telecommunicators will take this opportunity to use imagination and innovation in the provision of services that would benefit from deregulation. Clearly, the new directions we are proposing will help us reach our main goals for tomorrow in the areas of telecommunications and broadcasting.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be taking part in a debate that will undoubtedly be the first of many on telecommunications, an area for which the Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse) is responsible. I know he has quite a number of plans, and it will be
CRTC Act
very interesting to hear about these new developments concerning deregulation and the Government's new powers to issue directions.
I was listening carefully to the Minister, and I would like to start my comments by wishing him the very best in his new capacity as Minister over a vital sector of this country's economy. I think Canadians are not sufficiently aware of the importance of culture in Canada and of what we refer to as our cultural industries. The Minister himself is a man of considerable distinction and culture, and today again, he impressed the House with his wide-ranging historical knowledge, his quotes from Montesquieu and Cardinal Richelieu, and quite frankly, I think I would rather not try to follow him over the same terrain, because of the obvious political risk involved.
I must say the Minister was both reassuring and a little unsettling. What we see here... I am not going to provide a history of the CRTC, I think the Minister of Communications has already done so quite admirably. I am trying to be as politically objective as possible, so since I agree with what the Minister said, I do not see why I should repeat it. It was a more or less straightforward history of radio and television broadcasting in Canada and the power of the governors. It is only normal that the Minister should give his Party a front seat, since he told us in committee that he was a worthy son of the Progressive Conservative Party. I am indeed aware of his affiliation with this great Party which has done a great deal for Canada, but I also know that the Minister is a product of another political party we have known, and that is the Union Nationale. I will therefore try to steer a middle course between the two and maintain a federalist and prudent stance in my comments to the Minister of Communications.
Mr. Speaker, what struck me is that no mention was made of one of his predecessors, the Hon. Francis Fox to whom I can now refer by name because if we examine carefully the present text of Bill C-20 and compare it to the Bill tabled by Mr. Fox on February 8, 1984, we see that the work done by Mr. Fox is being continued by this Government today. In fact, the original Bill, tabled on February 8, 1984, was far broader in scope.
Again I say that I have no particular objection to the fact that the Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse) has asked that this very complex Bill be split. Indeed, Mr. Francis Fox had in fact introduced an omnibus Bill since it had to do with telecommunications, TV broadcasting, the Canadian Film Development Corporation Act and the Radio Act. I expect the Minister will eventually introduce other Bills concerning those Acts. In the same measure, Communications Minister Fox had also introduced on February 8, 1984-as it happened, it was also Bill C-20-another part concerning the reorganization of Bell Canada. I think the Minister is quite justified in including

January 31, 1985
CRTC Act
that subject matter under a separate piece of legislation, Bill C-19.
We will not argue about that except to say that, as I am expected, and it is not always easy, I have made a comparative study of both measures, what I would call the Masse project and the Fox project, to find out where they differ. I will therefore make a few remarks on the differences I found after scrutinizing both Bills.
As I said, Part I of this Bill is roughly the same as Part II of Bill C-20 introduced by Mr. Francis Fox and which relates to the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission Act. In his press release dated February 8, 1984, he explained that this part of Bill C-20-let us call it the Fox project-would amend the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission Act. For Hon. Members who might be interested, I have here this piece of legislation which was given Royal Assent on June 19, 1975. Since the Minister saw fit to refer to the good deeds of the Conservative Government, I might say that it was given Royal Assent on June 19, 1975, under a Liberal Government. I simply had to point that out to the Minister.
That Act amends, and I quote: "So as to enable the Governor in Council to issue general directions to the Commission, subject to certain limitations and considerations by Parliament. It also enables the Governor in Council to give executory directions to the CRTC concerning any question within its jurisdiction, except the issuance of a broadcasting licence to a particular person, or the amendment or renewal of a particular broadcasting licence".
I was going to say that the more things change, the more they remain the same. The bill would also require that the guidelines be tabled in Parliament and referred to a parliamentary committee for consideration. These guidelines would come into effect only 30 days after being tabled.
In this regard, I must tell the Minister that when the bill goes to the committee, and I have always said that I prefer the in-depth work done by parliamentary commissions, I shall have very specific questions to ask to find out what this means, because, as those who know parliamentary commissions in Ottawa will be aware-I prefer the term "parliamentary commission" used in Quebec to "parliamentary committee"- this bill will be examined thoroughly, and I shall insist on knowing exactly what the authors of the bill mean when they say that these guidelines will not come into effect until 30 days after they have been laid before Parliament.
What will happen if, when this bill is passed, as it will certainly be, the Minister takes advantage of an emergency, acting in good faith of course, to table guidelines in Parliament at a time when Parliament is not sitting, which can very often be the case? We have to know how this period of 30 days will apply. Will it be 30 days after the tabling of the guidelines or
30 days after parliamentarians have begun their examination? We shall look at this in detail in committee.
On the other hand, Bill C-20 as introduced by the Hon. Minister of Communications creates a new authority, which is described as follows in the press release of the Department of Communications dated December 20, 1984: " ... authorizing the Governor in Council to order the CRTC to deregulate competitively provided telecommunication services, and even to direct the Commission to refrain from exercizing its powers and performing its duties and functions."
All this will be accomplished under Section 14.6 to which the Minister has referred and which was not included in the legislation introduced by the Hon. Mr. Fox. Until we obtain some explanation in committee, we can only wonder whether the new Minister of Communications and his government want greater power than their predecessors had planned, because those who remember Mr. Fox, and I shall say something positive about him, which does not necessarily mean that I want to be critical of the new Minister, will know that Mr. Fox had the reputation of consulting and of taking action only after a genuine consensus had been reached.
I listened to the debate today. The Minister said that he would have extensive consultations which would be taken into account. I certainly hope so because many people have written to my leader, the Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) and to the Hon. Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse) with copies to myself, and I have to reply to all of them. It is not easy. I have to write to Mr. Bureau, to Mr. Juneau and to the Right Hon. Prime Minister, without mentioning all the letters which came to me directly in my capacity as critic for my party. These people wonder why there were cutbacks without prior consultation. I have to take the word of the Minister. Politically, it is dangerous to pay compliments because you have to live with them later. I can see my whip over there, but I shall pay the Minister a compliment anyway. I trust that the Minister believes in consultations. I am confident of this. Until I am proven wrong, I always give people the benefit of the doubt.
However, we have to look at what happened since November 8. I was in Halifax last Sunday, and I must say that, addressing more than a 1,000 people there, was not an easy task for the Hon. Member for Halifax. I congratulate him. I think that he might appreciate it. The Hon. Member for Halifax (Mr. Mclnnes) did very well under very difficult circumstances. He was obviously embarrassed-because his audience was not really warm nor very sympathetic to the cause he had to defend-to tell them. Yes, we have to make cutbacks and we shall have to make more.
But all those people from the Nova Scotia Coalition on Federal Policy also told me . . . I will spare you the list of names. I have them all, and the program is in English because when things get somewhat involved, sometimes everything is in English. There are authors, writers, performers, visual arts
January 31, 1985

crafts, art educators, Museum Galleries Heritage Societies, film makers, musicians, National Film Board, Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and that extraordinary, that remarkable man, that author from D'Escousse, Cape Breton, Silver Donald Cameron, and Mr. Curtis Barlow, the President of the Canadian Conference of the Arts, who, by the way, is most anxious to have an elaborate meeting with the Minister. He told me how difficult it was, but he is an important man in Canada. He represents a whole group of Canadians who are interested in our great cultural industry. And I must tell you, Mr. Minister, that he is still waiting for an interview and that he would very much appreciate being consulted. I hope such consultation promised by the Minister will actually take place.
As I said earlier, the Hon. Francis Fox was very successful in getting closer to those "milieus" which are not easy ones. The Minister knows it now, because the creativity milieu is a very sensitive one. It is a milieu that creates so many things but often it is under the impression that it is getting little in return, because it is ignored in many Canadian environments. I would like to be their spokesman, their advocate, and I know the Minister will do it. I know it is also the case with my hon. friends, my hon. friend who was also in Halifax. The NDP critic, he was in Halifax also. Those people feel they are giving much to Canadian society, and they also feel, rightly I assume, that they receive much less in return.
Therefore, considering this ever-increasing control exercised by this Government over the CRTC by way of its new powers to regulate, we have a right to be somewhat doubtful. So I will stick to that for the moment.
No doubt this is why I noticed the Hon. Mr. Crombie, who had given very good support, along with the Speaker and Mr. Geoff Scott, and I mention their names because I remember what they said and then their names were used. Yes, this came from the Progressive Conservative Party, with respect to the independance of federal-cultural agencies, as stated in the Canadian Arts Conference Bulletin, September-October 1984 edition. This is not from me, it is from the Hon. Crombie, the Hon. Bosley, our distinguished Speaker, and Mr. Geoff Scott. They said, and I quote:
We are convinced that the agencies and councils must be protected from changes in political outlooks, bureaucratic theories and expenditure priorities. We are now ready to translate into facts the efforts we made while we were in the Opposition-
-at the time. That is a statement which was made by my hon. friend opposite or at least signed by him.
-by implementing five year plans and formal mechanisms of consultation-
I repeat that we have indeed been promised this consultation process. I am going to tell in a non partisan way to all those hundreds of people who have written to me that I have received their testimony and that I now speak on their behalf in the House.

Well, we are told on page 6 that there will be consultations.
I will follow up on this. The Minister has made this commitment today and, knowing me, he knows that I am not the type to cause useless trouble, but I submit most respectfully that we have every right to remind the House that we have been promised consultations, as we intend to do in all civility, and I will be here to do so.
I should like to say that Part II of Bill C-20 corresponds to Part III of Bill C-20 which had been introduced by Hon. Mr. Fox and which dealt with the Broadcasting Act. I always return to Hon. Mr. Fox who, in his press release dated February 8, 1984, explained his proposed amendments to the Broadcasting Act. Because I know that some Hon. Members are interested, having asked me for it, I have brought to the House the Broadcasting Act which was adopted in 1967. For the information of the Minister who stated that three good things came out under a Conservative administration, I think that was under that great Prime Minister, the Right Hon. Lester Person, who I had the honour to know, having been elected twice to the House of Commons during his term, and to whom I am most grateful for having given to us this extraordinary Canadian flag which will be twenty years old on February 15, I hope that we will then unanimously pay tribute to our flag, for believe me, we were hardly unanimous in supporting this initiative in 1965!
The explanation given by Mr. Fox was as follows:
(A)	Redefine broadcasting and take into account recent technological developments to allow the CRTC to regulate the distribution of satellite signals;
(B)	Allow the CRTC to issue licenses for the operation of broadcasting companies; and
(C)	Redefine the role of society ... etc.-
I note that section 3 of the Broadcasting Act has been considerably altered. We need to know why, but that question will be asked on some later occasion.
The question dealt with in section 17 of Bill C-20 introduced by the Hon. Mr. Fox is similar to sections 3 and 4 in the bill tabled by the Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse). Moreover, section of Bill C-20 reflects the comments made by the Hon. Mr. Fox on May 24, 1984 when he gave this very important explanation:
The responsibility, as far as the contents of programming is concerned, rests with the broadcaster in accordance with the regulations of the CRTC ... This amendment will indeed make explicit the Government's commitment to the principle that all Canadians have the right to programming which respects the dignity and equality of individuals and groups.
This is how 1 understand programming which, in a given context, does not discriminate against the individual on the basis of race, national or ethnic origin, religion, sex, age, physical or mental disability
So, there is nothing new under the sun. I was under the impression a while ago ... a colleague who just arrived told me: "But it is a new dynamic legislation." I had to reply: "Well, no, the minister has divided the bill. It is almost the same provisions and the same wording". We are not offended but it should be acknowledged that our bill was excellent since

January 31, 1985
CRTC Act
the new government which was democratically elected with a large majority-and I accept this decision-has decided to reintroduce it. But the minister has announced nothing new.
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to note that those are exactly the same words used in paragraph Cl.l of the text now introduced by the Minister of Communications. Moreover, that amendment had been supported by the Minister responsible for the Status of Women, the Hon. Judy Erola. And, still according to Mr. Fox, the amendment, and I quote: "would provide a more clearly defined basis for the regulatory measures to be taken by the CRTC, to ensure that the broadcasting system contributes toward providing women and other groups with positive representation ..." I realize my New Democratic Party colleague will want to elaborate on this issue and I will let her do so, because I know how boring it is for Hon. Members to listen to the debate and then have to repeat what was said. To continue my quote: "without however impinging on the freedom of speech provided under the Broadcasting Act or the provisions of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms introduced by the previous Liberal Government."
The Hon. Francis Fox ... I feel he is still with us here in the House, and when I see his distinguished successor here today, I still have the impression that Mr. Fox is there because I am hearing more or less what he said when I read at the end of the Minister's press release: The Government hereby intends to respond to the concerns formulated by Canadians with respect to the impact of pornography and content with abusive tendencies, by giving the regulatory agency the power to act if necessary. I see that I wrote "careful" in my text at this point. Which means: do not exaggerate, but the fact is, there are people in Canada who tend to exaggerate. I would not want anyone to conclude that the Merchant of Venice is pornography. There is always the matter of balance, and I am sure that when the Minister issues his directions-when the Act will allow him to do certain things it does not allow him to do right now-he will keep that in mind.
Mr. Fox's comments, of course, preceded the press release by the Minister of Communications, who explains his legislation as follows:
In the recent Throne Speech, the Government of Canada reiterated that dealing with the problem of sexually abusive broadcasting remained one of its priorities. The purpose of the proposed amendment to the Broadcasting Act which concerns this kind of programming is to allay public concern and follow up the recommendations in the report of the Parliamentary Sub-committee on Sexually Abusive Broadcasting, published in June 1984.
I have the distinct impression that the Minister and I... have been consulting each other. He said as much, so we agree.
We shall therefore be able to discuss in committee the extent of our agreement on the proposal in Clause 5 which is aimed at easing some of the regulatory burden and the provisions imposed by Clause 6. The Minister will therefore know my position when we get to the committee stage.
I think that at this point I will forego some of the further comments I was going to make, but I would like to add that Mr. Fox's plan also included changes in the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. However, I suppose the Minister will get back to us on that in another Bill, and we will be ready to tackle that aspect when he does. The House will also recall that the Minister said there would be consultations and new regulations. So for the benefit of us senior Parliamentarians and for the benefit of the Minister of Communications who is listening attentively and-I want to thank him for staying in the House-I would advise him to be careful, because in the press release it says that the Department of Communications, under the co-ordination-that is what it says-of three consultants will probably, that is what I say, be working in close co-operation with the task force chaired by the Deputy Prime Minister, the Hon. Eric Nielsen, to determine any other regulatory changes that are to be submitted.
Well, you can imagine that we senior Parliamentarians are going to be very careful, now we know that the Deputy Prime Minister as well can start issuing directions on the matter of regulations and have them adopted by his Minister of Communications. I want to point out that this was said at the meeting of the Committee chaired by Mr. Gabriel Fontaine on December 4, 1984. We shall therefore be very cautious in examining these new regulations, especially if the Hon. Deputy Prime Minister has anything to say about them.
Part III of Bill C-20 corresponds to Part V of the Bill introduced by the Hon. Mr. Fox and concerns the Radio Act. This is therefore a repetition of the legislation introduced by the predecessor of the Minister, the Hon. Mr. Fox. For those who want to take notes, I have the Radio Act before me. This new legislation could, and I say this to the Parliamentary Secretary as the Minister is temporarily absent-but I can see that he is trying to tell me something.
Mr. Speaker, as you know, many of us have introduced Private Members' Bills. I would like to mention a few of them in the hope that the Minister might want to examine these bills introduced by individual Members who then sat on the side of the opposition and who are now Government Members, and some introduced by the then critic for cultural affairs. The Minister might decide eventually to examine these bills introduced by his own colleagues to determine what should be done with them. Here are a few of them: Bill C-301, in the name of the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), Bill C-461, in the name of the Hon. Member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen), the new chairman of the International Parliamentary Union who, on this very day, is receiving the visit of the General Secretary of the Parliamentary Union to sign the contract which will allow us to host the world convention next September. This has happened before under a liberal administration and I was the chairman of that conference. I was the one to send the invitation, but it is my

friend the new chairman, the Hon. Member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta, who will open the world conference of parliamentarians in September 1985. I will attend as an observer rather than a participant, with some regret. But such is life in politics.
I also want to point out to the Minister that these bills reflect the need to protect young people against overly agres-sive publicity during childrens' programming. Since 1980, Members of Parliament have also made representations provincially to the CRTC. I refer to Bill C-595 introduced by the Hon. Member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Wenman). If Hon. Members want to look at these bills, I have found all of those introduced from 1980 to 1984.
There is also Bill C-413, introduced by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (M. Orlikow), who is the NDP critic for communications, I believe, which deals with equal broadcasting time for opposition political parties. Believe it or not, there is also legislation on the educational use of programming, which was introduced by your distinguished colleague from Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie), namely Bills C-236 and C-224. Of course, there is also Bill C-675 introduced by the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald), to forbid any discriminatory comment based on sex, which the Hon. Mr. Fox had already approved in a second statement made on May 24, 1984, amending his statement of February 8, 1984. If anyone wants to examine all these bills, I have them and I have also found the debates held about them.
I could go on. I do not want to waste the time of the House, but I believe I have a few minutes left. Bill C-20 will therefore be referred to the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture which the Minister said was his intention when he appeared before the Committee on December 4, 1984. Mr. Speaker, at that time, the Standing Committee will have the opportunity to examine this issue. As a matter of fact, I believe that the Chairman of the Committee is here now.
So I am giving advance notice. I do not see why I should not give him a week's notice. I am not anxious to take my witness by surprise, something lawyers like to do. So the kind of witnesses we might... of course the Government will have its own witnesses, and the New Democratic Party, but I would like to mention their names, and I think the Minister may be surprised. These are not surprise witnesses, but they are very well known, and probably the best known of the ones on my first list is Prof. John Meisel of Queen's University, who might be invited to appear before the committee. I have a lengthy biography here, but I will spare the House the details. We may be able to get the committee to agree to invite Mr. Alan Borovoy of the General Council of the Canadian Civil Liberties Association of Toronto, whose reputation is certainly well-established, as the Toronto Star of November 8, 1983 said in a full-page article on Mr. Borovoy, the wellknown champion and defender of civil rights. So if anyone wants to know who the witness is . . . Mr. Speaker, perhaps we could
CRTC Act
also invite Mr. Fox, since today's Bill is so similar to the one he tabled in the House. There is a possibility. I am not saying we must, but he will certainly be on my list. Of course, there will be CRTC representatives. And I think it would be very unfortunate if we were deprived of the presence of the Minister himself. I am not going to put him on my list since it is obvious he will be the principal witness. We could also agree to invite representatives of the Canadian Association of Broadcasters, the Communications Workers of Canada, the FTQ, the Canadian Cable Television Association and experts in various fields, and listen to their representations. I have received submissions from people who would like to appear, but that will have to keep for some other time, because the submissions do not directly relate to this Bill. However, perhaps we will have the Alliance of Canadian Cinema, Television and Radio Artists, the Association of Canadian Film Craftspeople, the Association of Canadian Film and Television Producers-I will spare you the rest of the list.
The Minister tells us there will be new directions. We will have to ensure that these directions do not stifle the powers of the CRTC. I know the Minister of Justice has decided to listen to those people who advised him not to prosecute in cases that had been taken up by the CRTC. The House may remember a statement published in The Globe and Mail on November 24, 1984, in which the Minister of Justice actually boasted he was prosecuting some of the people who were finally being prosecuted by the CRTC. However, I understand that since then, the Minister has been conducting exhaustive inquiries across the country, and considering this fact, I admit that the arguments I intended to put forward today will therefore have to be toned down somewhat. I also want to congratulate the Minister for having a staff that is able to provide objective information. Thanks to the Minister's staff, I do not have to be as fierce as I intended on this particular issue. In fact, I think the Minister ought to know I found out about these consultations through his staff. However, the fact remains that these cases are not being prosecuted and that they should be. My colleague, the Justice critic and Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan) referred to this matter, and for those who are interested, I may refer them to page 681 of Hansard, November 28, 1984, when there was a fairly lively exchange of views.
I have been informed that at the last federal-provincial conference, the provincial ministers wanted the Government of Canada to have more authority over the CRTC, and that is probably why Bill C-20 and its predecessor deal with this problem. The Minister is aware that it is a problem, because we want the CRTC to operate without undue political interference, the provincial authorities want to express their views at the political level and we must also respect the rights guaranteed under our Constitution.
I realize that the Minister has to perform a balancing act, probably because his Department is among those that are

January 31, 1985
CRTC Act
directly involved in this issue. He is expected to remain at arm's length, yet he is being asked to intervene. We will see in the next few years just how the Minister will manage to keep his balance. In any event, I can tell him as kindly as I can that we will be there to help him.
As you may understand, Mr. Speaker, people are deeply concerned. There were so many cut backs without prior consultation, but here they are today telling us that consultations there will be. As official critic responsible for doing that job honourably and honestly, I am in a dilemma which I might make even worse if I were to insist by pouring salt on wounds which the Minister finds very difficult to dress these days. He is under attack from every quarter because of those cut backs about which he probably did not have much to say.
I have no idea whether the Minister made the necessary representations to the Minister of Finance and told him: No, you can cut... but you cannot cut people who give so much and receive so little. Those people give much to our country, they make us proud and they give us our Canadian identity. That is what we must understand. There are two major survival movements in Canada. God knows that francophones are aware of the word "survival" and of the French fact. Yet the Minister must also realize that English Canada has a morbid fear of americanization. That is why the Minister should not and will not be surprised to find such a reaction in English Canada.
I know, and we are going to do our best to make people understand why it is that English-speaking Canadians are deeply concerned about americanization. That is why deregulation is a good thing, but it must not be carried to extremes either. We do need some protection. If we want our own Canadian culture-English or French-we must have safeguards, Mr. Speaker, for our neighbours can be intrusive indeed.
I want to assure the Minister that he can count on my cooperation in committee where this Bill will soon be under consideration. subtopic: CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising to address the Bill before us, Bill C-20. It is a very modest Bill in its size but that is not to say the matters it deals with are not important. There are principles at stake in this Bill, a small number of them, which for the most part are not going to be partisan or controversial. Most of the measures before us today we have seen before in the legislation which appeared last year but was not passed.
While they have their importance, given the recent cutbacks of and interference in the operations of the CBC, 1 must express some concern and frustration that we are not dealing with the more important matters facing us in the area of broadcasting. It is perhaps not fiddling while Rome burns, but I am a bit concerned that we are fiddling while Rome is closing down its stations and firing creative staff.
Those of us who are committed to a strong and vital broadcasting system in Canada know that it can be achieved only with a very strong public component in the CBC. Of course, that public component has to be adequately funded so it can do its job in both languages in television, and AM and FM radio. These are matters which we will have to address, so I look forward to the next discussion the Minister will bring forward perhaps even more so than discussing the matters before us in this Bill. We have to get into broadcasting policy and adequate funding if the system we are now amending is going to function in the way we want it to.
As to the specific provisions of Bill C-20, Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin with Clause 14.1. We certainly support these proposals. This will allow the Minister to issue policy directives to the CRTC. It is important that the Minister not have the power to intervene regarding particular applications before the CRTC, and there are safeguards in the Bill to ensure that.
I have had some concerns raised with me that these safeguards are not strong enough and perhaps the wording will have to be looked at in committee, but as to the principle, it is a sound one. The Minister is responsible to Parliament for broadcasting policy and he then responds to Parliament, comes before the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture and answers for those policy directives. That is all part of our parliamentary system.
I now want to get on to the deregulation provisions proposed in Clause 14(6). These are provisions which we do not approve of in the Bill. We oppose those measures. Incidentally, they were not part of the old Bill which was before the House last year. This provision would give very broad powers to the Minister, expand them in an unacceptable way, to say that there would be no regulation in a certain area. This supposedly
January 31, 1985

on the grounds that competition is adequate to look after the matter.
I just do not have enough confidence that the public interest will be well served with this very broad power of deregulation, which has been the trend in the United States. We have certainly already seen some very bad repercussions from that. We have a rather difficult situation here and it is quite different from the U.S. We have to be very careful of the public interest. Certainly the economics go against the Canadian broadcasting system, but we are already overwhelmingly foreign influenced in this area where monopolies operate and competition is severely limited. That means all the more power must be retained by the CRTC to ensure that the public interest is kept at the forefront.
To get on to some of the other measures, Clause 2 in Part II and Clause 7 in Part III are measures which would clarify the definition of a broadcasting undertaking in television and radio respectively. Clearly these will assert regulatory control for master antenna satellite dishes in areas such as hotels, condominiums and large apartments. We are concerned that individual households and small apartments be able to operate without regulation, but we certainly approve of the changes in order to bring regulatory control to this area and close a loophole in the law. This would simply serve to clarify a situation which should have been dealt with earlier, so we support these measures.
Another part of Part II refers to a matter being dealt with by a CRTC task force, which will be reporting early in February on the difficulties experienced by small and isolated communities in receiving broadcasting signals. This is a matter dealt with in the legislation. If the recommendations from this task force are adequate and suitable, perhaps they could be introduced at committee stage and incorporated in the legislation. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) will be addressing this matter in more detail later.
I have some reservations about another measure contained in Part II, Clause 5(1). This is a new measure to increase the period of licence from five years to seven years. This is somewhat in the spirit of deregulation. It makes regulation less effective by giving stations and networks licences for a longer period. They are, in effect, less accountable to the regulatory authority. This is not just an idle or academic matter. I think of the time when the CRTC licensed pornographic programming in pay television. It said that it did it by mistake. It had certainly been warned about the problem, but in effect it did give licences and discovered later what was involved in that. When it was criticized for this and the problem was brought to its attention, its response was that there was nothing it could do about it for five years because that was the period of licence and the time to address the problem was when the licence expired. Five years is a very long period of time for a licence. I would have reservations about increasing that period of time to seven years.
CRTC Act
Let us be clear on the process of intervention at the CRTC. Intervention at the CRTC is one of the more popular sports in Canada. There is a very enjoyable atmosphere and an opportunity for individuals and groups to appear. In short, the democratic process is alive. The CRTC, in its ivory tower and all its distance, majesty and wealth, actually comes before the public and asks what it has to say about policy and what it wants to see in broadcasting. The public-individuals, specialists and groups-come with their concerns. This is a very healthy part of our regulatory process. Women's groups have used this process to protest sex stereotyping in the media and the pornography issue. The hearings have been very important in regard to religious broadcasting, children's broadcasting, and other areas in which the public has a vital interest and a great deal of knowledge. This very healthy process would be weakened by extending the length of time of licences. Rather than treating the public cynically and avoiding talking and listening to it for seven years, this intervention should be welcomed. The Canadian public, for which the broadcasting system exists, does have a positive contribution to make. It does this very effectively through interventions to the CRTC.
I would like to move on to the issue of the amedments in clause 3 of the Bill. These amendments were brought in as result of my Private Member's Bill C-675. That Bill was debated last year and referred to committee. There was unanimous agreement from the sub-committee which studied the Bill to making an amendment, which unfortunately could not be legislated before the House finished its work in June of last year. It is before us today in wording which is not exactly to my liking, but which is acceptable and will accomplish what is necessary. This is to add to Section 3, the purpose section of the Broadcasting Act, a new Section 3. (c.l). It reads:
The programming provided by the Canadian broadcasting system should respect and promote the equality and dignity of all individuals, groups or classes of individuals regardless of race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex, age or mental or physical disability;
This is a very general proviso. It is stated in very general terms. It says "should" not "must". It gives a purpose which is consistent with the purpose section of the Broadcasting Act. It refers only to programming in general. It does not stipulate every program. It is not a very specific measure, but it does set out a purpose of some importance to us.
For this purpose to have effect there must be more detailed regulation on the matter. The CRTC has in fact introduced a regulation to that effect. The CRTC was very slow in responding to the problem of violent and severely degrading pornography. However, it did finally act and bring in a regulation. Once the CRTC was convinced we discovered that it was the Department of Justice that was holding back and causing problems. The CRTC was prepared to move faster. Therefore, it can be convinced. This regulation is in place which obviously must be if the purpose section of the Act is to have any effect.
I would like to bring the attention of the House to the omission of something which I think should be included. In my Private Member's Bill there was a clause which said that notwithstanding the provisions of Section 3, being the freedom

January 31, 1985
CRTC Act
of expression provisions, this more specific prohibition of abusive broadcasting would hold. The existence of a similar "notwithstanding" clause in the legislation would make it clear that we as legislators are perfectly well aware of the freedom of expression objective, and that we are qualifying it to ensure that another fundamental principle, that is, the dignity and equality of all people, is also respected. It would be clear that this is a qualification. It is not that we are disregarding freedom of expression, but that we admit that another principle is of considerable importance.
This section will undoubtedly be a matter of appeal to the courts. There will be people who will go to the courts and use the freedom of expression provisions of the Charter of Rights as their defence. I think it is important to give the courts guidance on this. I have a very specific reason for recommending that. Canadian courts have been notoriously bad on equality issues. They have been even worse when the equality was claimed by women rather than by any other group. There has been a long history from the Persons case to Laval and Bedard and Murdoch. These cases have shown that the courts have been insensitive to equality rights for women. It would be prudent to give very clear guidance to the courts that the equality and dignity of all people must be respected. There is a good reason for including this in the Bill.
[Translation)
The Reseau d'action et d'information sur les femmes had this to say before the sub-committee on sexually abusive broadcasting, which studied the subject matter of my bill, and I quote:
Since our organization now has a charter that not only clearly asserts equality between the sexes but also provides for means to correct the harm done to women, it follows logically that broadcasting must conform to that new justice and that all abuse against sexual equality must be eliminated.
Therefore, this amendment to the Act contained in the legislation now before the House is a logical consequence of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
I would like to thank all the Canadian men and women who supported me in requesting such an amendment to the Act. A very large number of Canadian men and women from all parts of Canada and from all parties in Canada have fought for better protection against violent and degrading pornography. They have fought as individuals and as groups, as feminists and as mothers and fathers. I would like especially to mention the participation of the Quebec Federation of Women, Media Watch, the National Action Committee on the Status of Women, the Reseau d'action et d'information sur la femme, the Front commun contre la pornographic, the Churches, the Catholic Women's League, specialists from the universities and the professions of Canada who helped us during the sub-committee meetings.
We have realized that the attacks against women and children by means of violent and degrading pornography are attacks against the equality and dignity of all human beings. The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms guarantees
equality for all Canadian men and women. Any kind of programming that infringes upon the dignity and equality of any part of humanity is an aggression against the value and dignity of all of humanity.
I am pleased to support this Bill in principle. Although we do want to see some changes in committee, we agree with the majority of its contents. The changes we would like can be made in committee. We will offer our support for this Bill as well as our co-operation during its study in committee.

subtopic: CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is one particular aspect of this Bill to which I want to refer. It is the amendments to the Radio Act and the Broadcasting Act relating to regulating broadcasting in this country. The change to extend licences from five to seven years is quite interesting. The Minister explained that change in his opening statement.
The Bill gives the Government and thereby the people of Canada additional power to regulate or control the CRTC and the operations of radio broadcasting in this country. I wonder what powers the Minister or the CRTC have under the present legislation to prevent the closure of radio stations.
In the decisions which were made solely by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, it closed one radio station in all of its cuts across the country. My concern is that there appears to be no recourse unless the Minister were to include in his recommendations to the House for regulatory control that the CBC or any radio network must appear before the CRTC for a public hearing. I have two reasons for that opinion. When licences are granted by the CRTC to establish radio stations in small communities, that licence is granted upon the intent of the operator to provide full service. Occasionally, for obvious economic reasons, the operator finds it more reasonable to reduce that station to just a transmitter. Throughout the country we have seen the CBC do this and consolidate in certain areas and simply carry a signal on what is called low-power relay transmitters.
In other words, if the CBC or other private broadcasters are permitted, there will eventually be a network of stations operating from one central area while claiming that they are providing the same service as if there were local news and communications people in the community. In other words, what you would hear on the CBC is: "You are listening to a network of CBC stations".
That certainly is not acceptable today and will not be acceptable in the future.
In order to illustrate exactly what I am talking about in reference to the Radio Act and the Broadcasting Act, let me
January 31, 1985

point out that there is a delegation in Ottawa who came all the way from Gander, Newfoundland. They are here to meet with the CBC. As well, I believe the Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse) was good enough to meet with them as well. They are protesting the closure of the CBC radio station in their community. Since its personnel are being moved to another location, the saving to the corporation in real dollars is a measly $75,000 a year in operational costs for that particular building.
When one ask the CBC why it made that decision, it has some interesting explanations. I had a three-hour meeting with the President of the CBC and the director of radio for the country. They gave me this second option which I referred to earlier. That option is consolidation, which appears to be acceptable to private broadcasters and the CBC. They tried to prove to me that there would be a better service in a community if the radio station was 100 miles away.
During that briefing they produced the ratings. Those ratings show that the particular station the CBC was closing had the best ratings from 6 a.m. until 9 a.m. of the three regional stations. It had the best listening audience from noon until 2 p.m. and the best listening audience from 4 p.m. to 6.30 p.m. In other words, the CBC, which does not sell commercials on radio, was beating the two private networks in that area.
I suggested to the CBC representatives during the meetings that they should look at those ratings to determine if location was not the reason why the ratings are so high, and to suggest that if it followed the same course of action that it has taken in Vancouver and other parts of the country, perhaps the ratings would drop. The fact is that this CBC station which is to be closed has higher ratings than other networks. Where else in Canada does such a rating structure exist? I repeat that the CBC is doing this to save a mingy $75,000, with the excuse that the federal Government has cut back its budget. It says that it has a cut-back of $75 million and that it must close a station to save $75,000. What kind of logic is that?
The point of the matter is that this particular station covers an enormous geographic area; not only Gander but all of the northeast coast of Newfoundland and the central portion. If that station and its personnel is moved to another location, say 60 miles or 100 miles away, there will not be that community identification or the identification that the corporation had with the arts community, music community or with local events. Right now that station is able to report the last town council meeting at Badger's Quay or Joe Batt's Arm. Obviously if they were located in a centralized area, they could not do it. That is why the ratings are so high.
There is another consideration which I brought up in the House. I am sure each Member remembers CBG Gander. I brought up on one occasion that the terms of union with Canada were being violated by the decision to close down CBG. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation took over the radio stations that were in existence at the time of union in Newfoundland. It just so happens that CBG was in existence
CRTCAct
at Confederation. After looking at all of that, we still have no recourse. The people in that community have no recourse right now for a hearing before the CRTC. They have no recourse because the Minister says that he really does not want to interfere. I respect the Minister for that statement, Mr. Speaker. The Corporation obviously has to settle its own problems. I have difficulty-and you can go back over the records, Mr. Speaker-when I read what the Minister himself said in the House. As reported on page 1007 of Hansard for December 7, 1984, he said:
Since there was a risk that this administrative obligation would affect the CBC's general strategy and its long-term operations, I decided, in agreement with the President of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, that a consultation process was necessary.
Then he quoted a letter from Mr. Juneau which said that he agreed with this consultation process and that it was necessary. Then the Minister appointed three very able people and said that the senior officials worked together with "my special consultants". That is found on page 1007. subtopic: CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
The broadcasting industry is one of words, thoughts, aspirations and of Canadian definition. I think it is passing strange that the very delegation which travelled to Ottawa on Monday to plead about the public sector cultural cuts happens to do very handsomely indeed in the private sector. I think it fitting to remark that Mr. Berton, one of the leaders of that delegation, will be launching on February 1, tomorrow, a magnificent new private radio series called The Canadian Achievers. As an Albertan, I hesitate to say that the series is sponsored by Petro-Canada. It will focus on Canadian
heroes and achievers from all walks of life. This is private radio, Mr. Speaker, and it is an industry in which Mr. Berton and many of his allies do very well indeed. In a sense I think they are setting up un faux spectre, a straw man, a bogeyman, in trying to cry wolf in advance that there will be more cuts in the cultural and public communications sector.
It is time for a review of the entire Canadian broadcasting system. There have been many such reviews. I think it most fitting that the current review be taking place where it belongs and that is in the Parliament of Canada. I say that because we are the proper conduit of the will of the Canadian people toward the Canadian broadcasting system. The review is overdue because of the developments of technology and the rampant growth of the regulatory system in a legislative vacuum.
I should like to trace briefly the history of broadcast regulation in the country. Initially, regulation was deemed necessary in order to control frequency allocation in communication with ships and fishing boats at sea. Therefore, initially the regulation came under the ambit of the Department of Marine and Fisheries. Later it passed to the Canadian Radio Broadcasting Commission, the precursor of the CBC, which took the regulation of private broadcasting under its wing. The same principle obtained when the CBC came forward as a creation of the Bennett Government of the 1930s.
In 1958, in response to the demands of equitable treatment on the part of the private broadcasting industry which up to that point had been regulated by its commercial competitor, the CBC, the government of the day, under the leadership of the late Right Hon. John Diefenbaker, formed the Board of Broadcast Governors. It was the first independent regulatory authority to govern both the CBC and private industry. In turn, it was succeeded in 1968 by the current regulatory body which was then called the Canadian Radio-Television Commission and now embraces telecommunications as well.
A few moments ago I mentioned the vacuum which has existed for a number of years in the whole area of giving direction to the growth of the Canadian broadcasting system. This vacuum in which the CRTC has ben operating has resulted in some grotesque rulings and some questionable decisions. I cite just one or two of them. The decision to license various pay television enterprises, which was taken less than two years ago, is well known to Hon. Members of the House and to the Canadian public. It was a decision which had no basis in economics or in actual reality. We have seen the shepherded shrinking of that system to the point where we now have in essence in the English language just one system across the country.
In addition, there has been a rather disturbing trend toward the wholesale licensing of frequencies in various communities across Canada. I say that is unfortunate. I may be challenged by my NDP friends opposite in that I may be accused of not speaking for free enterprise and looking for a cushy environment. That is not the case at all. The fact of the matter is that in the United States, which is a terribly over-licensed country,
January 31, 1985

many stations do not have the resources to offer the kind and quality of public service for which the Canadian broadcasting system, both public and private, is justly famous.
As well, we have had a proliferation of questionable regulations in this legislative vacuum. That proliferation of regulations has led to quixotic and rather disturbing regulations being imposed and statements of policy being made by regulatory fiat, to the extent that third level interpreters of those regulations are dictating to Canadians what they will hear or see. In fact, they are determining in some cases what individual pieces of music are properly played by individual stations. That verges on an impingement on freedom of speech.
I should like to spend a moment outlining the provisions of Clause 1 of this Bill. The directive power which is proposed here would be used to ensure that the Government rather than the CRTC is responsible for setting telecommunications and broadcasting policy in the country. It could be used to establish general criteria by which the Commission could decide individual matters coming before it. In other cases it could be used to ensure that broad national policies on matters such as the economy are applied in broadcasting and telecommunications. Perhaps the pay television situation to which I referred earlier could be embraced within that.
One might ask what safeguards exist to prevent the Government from abusing the power of direction and from interfering with the rights of broadcasters to freedom of speech. The Charter of Rights and Freedoms would prohibit directions from impinging upon freedom of speech. As well, the Bill contains a clear limitation in that no policy directions may be issued in respect of the issue, amendment or renewal of a particular broadcasting licence. Further, the Bill provides for parliamentary scrutiny of directions before they take effect.
Mindful of the clock, I should like to make one or two further comments about Clause 5(1) and Clause 5(2) which deal with the extension of maximum licence terms. We have heard an Hon. Member opposite question the extension of the maximum term of licence from five years to seven years. The hon. lady suggested that perhaps Five years was too long a term of licence. We are talking about a pretty sizeable industry. Just as our nation is looking forward to having some consistency and predictability of policy, which the Government is now providing, so are the broadcasting industry and the cable industry looking for some kind of predictability whereby they can plan their affairs over a longer period of time.
We are talking about an industry which in the radio and television sector generates something over $1 billion of revenue per year, with $492 million in radio and $833 million in television. Of course, much of that is advertising revenue, virtually all of it. We are talking about a large number of employees-in the private radio sector of the industry alone, 9,666 and in the television sector, 6,905. We are talking about salaries well up into the hundreds of millions of dollars. We are talking about Fixed assets in the broadcasting sector alone of $637 million. In the cable sector, gross revenues in the most recent year of reporting were $535 million. The net proFit after tax was $34.2 million, which represented a 5.9 per cent return
on fixed assets of $579 million. The payroll of the cable industry is about $149 million, which represents 6,484 fulltime employees.
Predictability is absolutely essential. To add two years to the maximum licence term of five years is a measure which I am sure the industry and indeed the public will welcome. With predictability comes the potential of profitability. It is only from profitability in the private broadcasting industry that creative programming can come about, that jobs can be created, that the Canadian identity can be reinforced and that indeed public service can be enhanced.
