PAN-AMERICAN GAMES LONDON, ONT., ADVOCATED AS HOST CITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to make a statement about an historic decision made last week, a decision which I believe has the potential to bring great economic and social benefit to Canada. The Canadian Olympic Association has chosen London, Ontario, to be the Canadian city to host the Pan-American Games six years from now. It only remains for Canada to be chosen instead of the one other Pan-American country applying.
The economic benefit to London, to southwestern Ontario, and in a broader sense to Canada, of hosting these games has been conservatively estimated at $500 million. The Games will provide at least 150,000 days of work for construction workers, and an estimated 400 jobs for the period before, during, and after the games. I ask, therefore, that this House and the Government of Canada work to ensure that Canada is chosen to host these games so that this great tourist opportunity and all the other prodigious economic and social benefits will in fact flow to our country.

Mr. Speaker, agriculture can and does play a vital role in the rebuilding of our economy, but the Government wants to do it through consultation. Today, 160 farmers from Ontario are meeting with their MPs as part of this consultation process. This Government welcomes their advice, but it has already shown that it cares about agriculture. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) has already taken several initiatives to help alleviate the financial problems facing many farmers.
Thousands of FCC loans have been, or will be, re-written down to 12.75 per cent. Niagara grape growers have been made a part of a buy-up scheme. The 4.8 cent tax on gasoline and diesel fuel has been removed. The offshore labour program is in effect for 1985. Capital gain rollovers are now eligible for contributions to RRSPs.
While these programs indicate that agriculture has received top priority from the Government in only a few months, it does not intend to stop or sit still. The Government is working with the provinces to establish a tripartite stabilization program for red meat. Section 31 of the Income Tax Act is being examined, and agri-bonds will receive further study. The Government is prepared to move on these items.
No longer can the Government pay lip-service to agriculture, or let it take a back seat to other sectors of our economy. This Government is not prepared to sit by and let farmers suffer for another decade or two of neglect and despair. Agriculture is the backbone of our economy, and it is this Government's intention to stengthen that backbone even further, within its financial resources.

maintopic: EFFECT OF CHANGES ON PERSONNEL RETIRING FROM ARMED FORCES
EFFECT OF CHANGES ON PERSONNEL RETIRING FROM ARMED FORCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, over the past few weeks I have received scores of telephone calls from Armed Forces personnel who are concerned about the effect that the UI changes to earnings will have on them when they retire. Members of the Armed Forces are required to retire by the age of 55, or after 25 years of service.
One of the recognized and very much deserved benefits of serving with the Armed Forces is the accumulation of severance benefits. The Conservative Government has announced that, as of March 31, 1985, those payments will be considered as income for unemployment insurance purposes. I understand from the Minister's office that the rollover provisions that allow severance benefits to be placed into an RRSP, so that they will not be considered as income for income tax purposes, will not apply for UI purposes. This essentially wipes out the value of those severance payments that were formerly considered a working benefit.
Many of those who retire from the Armed Forces continue to work until the usual retirement age of 65, and continue to make UI contributions during those working years. The Government has announced that pension income will be considered income for UI purposes, essentially making those retirees ineligible for UI benefits. Due to the early retirement age of Armed Forces personnel, they have been placed in the very unique situation of being required to pay into an insurance program, the Unemployment Insurance Program, without being eligible to collect benefits from that program. I suggest to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) that these discriminatory aspects of UI changes should be reconsidered.

subtopic: REMOVAL OF CAPITAL GAINS TAX FROM FARM LAND SALES URGED
REMOVAL OF CAPITAL GAINS TAX FROM FARM LAND SALES URGED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for many years the farming community suffered under the heavy-handed regime of the former Liberal administration, supported by its'NDP allies.
The issue of capital gains has hung over the farming community and has created economic chaos and disunity among regions of Canada.
I commend our Government for a reduction in interest rates, which have declined 19 times in the past 19 weeks; a fuel tax rebate; a moratorium on Farm Credit Corporation foreclosures, and more recently a reduction to 12.75 per cent interest rates on over 5,600 FCC loans. As well, the Government has returned choice in the use of the metric system. I urge my Government to go one step further and remove the capital
gains tax from farm land sales in order to remove this dark cloud of uncertainty from the farm community.
Since this is a tax on the savings of a retiring farmer, a tax on the production of food, and adds greatly to the cost of land for a beginning farmer, I urge all Members of the House to support its immediate removal.

Mr. Speaker, it is a basic and fundamental principle of our criminal justice system that all persons be treated equally before the law and that one is presumed innocent until proven guilty. Tuesday's acquittal of Premier Richard Hatfield on a charge of possession of marijuana leads me to conclude that these basic principles have been breached.
The investigation leading to the charge and the subsequent prosecution raises a number of very disturbing questions. Why did the RCMP wait a month before charging Premier Hatfield? Was there political interference? When were the Solicitor General (Mr. MacKay) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) consulted? What instruction, if any, did they give to the RCMP? Is there any substance to the allegations that there was a cover-up attempt by the RCMP? Was it fair for the presiding judge unjustly and improperly to accuse a reporte of illegally planting the marijuana? Was Premier Hatfield given preferential treatment? Is there one law for the rich and powerful and another for the average citizen? More important, would a similar case involving a teenager from the other side of the tracks be dealt with in a similar fashion? I suspect not.
I call on the Solicitor General to conduct a complete and independent investigation into the investigation and prosecution of the matter, to clear the air, to ensure that the public continues to have confidence in the fairness of our criminal justice system, and to ensure that innocent persons are not harmed by a judge's irresponsible statements.
In my view, the case of the Queen versus Richard Hatfield was a grave miscarriage of justice.

Hear, hear!

speechtext: First of all, Mr. Speaker, I say to the Hon. Member that it pleases me very much to see where she and her Party are going. It is nice to know at this late date that that Party now believes that maybe Canada should be a partner in NATO.

the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence-

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Labour responsible for housing. The Minister has issued his consultation paper on housing in which he acknowledges that half a million tenant households cannot afford physically adequate and uncrowded housing, but he declares that the Government has no more money for housing and must redirect funds allocated to existing expenditure. Why does the Minister's report choose explicitly to ignore the billions of dollars paid out in tax expenditures to the large builders of rental accommodation when he calls for money to help those still in need?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I welcome the contribution I hope will be made by the Hon. Member to the consultation process which will go forward within the next two months. His specific question as to expenditures through rental accommodation for housing-providers is addressed by us. This Government, the previous administration, and Governments represented by the Hon. Member's Party-and I speak in particular of the Province of Manitoba-have the same process, the same assistance applied to provide rental accommodation for Canadian citizens. I know the Hon. Member is aware that in some of those accommodations there is a mixing of income groups, and a rent subsidy is offered to those who are in need.

Mr. Speaker, while the Minister did not answer my question about tax expenditures at all, I would like to ask him whether he has done studies on the shelter allowance proposals such as were put forward by the Canadian Homebuilders' Association? If so, will he make those studies available to Members of Parliament and the public?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation

Member, in looking at social benefits available to Canadians. I agree that shelter allowance should be considered one of those social benefits. Hopefully we will be discussing the issue further in the next two months during the consultation process.

Mr. Speaker, has the Minister consulted with his counterparts in the provincial Governments on the proposal by the Canadian Homebuilders' Association that rent controls should be removed in three years?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as the Hon. Member is aware, it is the autonomous provincial Governments which impose rent controls. I draw to his attention that rent controls have been removed in some provinces, but they continue in some eight jurisdictions. I suggest to the Hon. Member that such controls would be the prerogative of the provincial Governments, and that any impact they may have on the provision of housing to Canadians would have to be taken into consideration when the federal Government consults with its provincial colleagues.

subtopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF SECRETARY GENERAL OF THE INTER-PARLIAMENTARY UNION

speechtext: May I interrupt the proceedings to advise Members of the presence in our gallery today of Mr. Pio-Carlo Terenzio, Secretary General of the Inter-Parliamentary Union.

subtopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF SECRETARY GENERAL OF THE INTER-PARLIAMENTARY UNION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I, too, would like to address my questions to the Minister of National Defence and follow up on the somewhat curious logic of his argument when he says we are only negotiating a warning system, as confirmed by the Secretary of State for
External Affairs. The logic there is that once the warning system is in place and we see an incoming Cruise missile or bomber, we will wave at it as it goes by, because they are not talking about the other component, which is how to respond.
Obviously the Americans are planning a new North Ameri-an defence system and we want to know what the Government is doing to respond to that major change in U.S. strategy relating to North America? According to their official spokesman, they are planning a new defence program in the northern part of North America, including Canada. What in God's name are you doing about it? Are you thinking about it? Are you discussing it with them, or are you going to do something about it so that Canadians will know what the implications are?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert C. Coates (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, what my hon. friend is suggesting is that his Party, and the Government with which he was associated, allowed Canada to be placed in a situation where we did not even have a warning system to tell us if weapons were going to be coming into Canada from the U.S.S.R. At least we are going to put North America in a position where we will have a warning system to know that those weapons are coming in, if that should happen. The guarantee for Canadians is that if we have the warning system there is less likelihood that any weapons will be sent into our air space.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Defence said it all. He just does not know what is going on.

Mr. Speaker, I think it is very important that we get a commitment from the Government that the Prime Minister will not be signing any agreement with the President on a new warning system until the implications are clearly spelled out for our country in terms of major new expenditures on some form of defence program in North America. As well, we would need to know what the commitment would be regarding the placement of interceptor aircraft, or ground to air missiles, or any form of surveillance. We would also like a commitment that the Minister of Defence try to find out what is going on in North America so that we can properly defend ourselves.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert C. Coates (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, certainly when they were in the Government there was no way we could properly defend ourselves. The one thing they did do was to enter into an agreement to buy CF-18 aircraft. But what is the value of having CF-18 aircraft if we do not have a warning system which tells us when things are moving into our air space?

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Indian Affairs who, I know, is aware of the dangerous and growing conflict on Meares Island in British Columbia. Would the Minister take this opportunity to assure the Clayoquot and Ahousaht bands that they, in fact, hold title on Meares Island and he will immediately initiate negotiations with the Government of B.C. to resolve this conflict?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Hon. Member is,
I am sure, aware, the federal Government has accepted the land claim for negotiation. That is a fact. The Government of British Columbia and the two Indian bands concerned are aware of that, and I do not have to assert that. Let me also say that I am very aware of the difficulty on Meares Island and the possible explosiveness of the situation. I want to assure him that I will take whatever steps I can to be of assistance.

Mr. Speaker, Louis Riel was hanged 100 years ago for standing up for the rights of Indian people, particularly in relation to land title. Will the Minister take this opportunity to assure the Nuu-chah-nulth tribal Council that he will immediately appoint a negotiator so that there is at least a process in place to resolve this conflict which may bring about bloodshed and the return of a Duck Lake tragedy?

speakeroldname: Hon. David Crombie (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
As I indicated to the Hon. Member on a previous occasion, Mr. Speaker, since the matter has been accepted for negotiation the bands know where the federal Government stands on the matter. We will be proceeding to negotiation through a negotiator, at the appropriate time, in the normal way.
With respect to the problem on Meares Island, that is a matter which has to be dealt with, not only by the courts but, as I indicated to the Hon. Member, I am going to try to be of assistance in an informal way over the weekend.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. The Government has launched another attack on the family through its proposals on family allowance and the child tax exemption. The Minister is now suggesting that maternity benefits be removed from the unemployment insurance program. Does the Minister think it is fair to women, who have paid in for these benefits, for him even to think of tampering with this earned benefit?

Mr. Speaker, let me make it very clear again to the Hon. Member that there is no intention of removing that benefit. We are talking about how that benefit should be financed. As she knows, the benefit is now financed through the unemployment insurance scheme. We are suggesting that we should consider whether that financing should be done through the general tax system in order to allow for a lower payroll tax on small businesses to allow them to create more jobs.

I have a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker.
Again, financial security is of paramount importance for Canadians who want to raise a family. How can the minister justify modifying the unemployment insurance program by abolishing maternity benefits without any consultation? Why

January 31, 1985
Oral Questions
has he not tabled a White Paper on the issue instead of spreading fear among women? Is that equality, Mr. Minister?

Mr. Speaker, let me make it perfectly clear that what I have suggested is something which was put forward in the agenda paper last November. There has been lots of opportunity for people to discuss this. There will be opportunity in the future as we proceed with the consultations.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Justice. Last year the former Prime Minister, Mr. Trudeau, was justifiably criticized for not releasing his position on aboriginal rights in the Constitution until one day prior to the actual commencement of that conference. Can the Minister of Justice tell us when the new Conservative Government will make public its position on aboriginal rights in the Constitution?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman could not have been noticing that before Christmas we had a conference of Ministers of Justice. My colleague, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, was at the conference with the provinces and representatives of the aboriginal peoples. I think we made our position on the issues pretty clear to them. They were satisfied with the progress that was made.
When the constitutional conference takes place on April 2 and 3 the Prime Minister will have a well articulated well thought out position which we think will please the aboriginal peoples, Members of the House, and the people of Canada. There is much work being done. Just because we are not out in public every day discussing it or yelling about it, does not mean it is not being done. In addition-I don't want to be long. Mr. Speaker. In addition-
Good. The Hon. Member for Churchill on a supplementary question.
Mr. Speaker, I am not worried about the length of the answer. I am worried about the fact that he will not give us that information before the conference.

Can the Minister assure us that we are not going to have a repeat of last year's conference when the provincial Governments could quite rightfully say that they did not have the information early enough? Is the information going to be made public well in advance of the commencement of the conference?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am glad to be able to reassure the hon. gentleman on that point. Last year the then Government tried a game of one-upmanship and was not telling anyone what it was doing. Neither the provinces nor the aboriginal peoples knew what it would place on the table at any moment. We have committed ourselves to keep the provinces and the aboriginal peoples well informed ahead of time of what our proposals will be. They have promised to do the same with us. They are well satisfied with the way they are now being treated. There is no complaint that I am aware of, except in the enfeebled mind of the hon. gentleman.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. Prince Edward Island is dependent on ferry service in order to move people, goods, and services. The Island and Nova Scotia are served well by Northumberland Ferries Ltd., although growing concern exists due to long waits, current hours of service, and high rates. Will the Minister assure the House that his Department will negotiate with the provincial Government and Northumberland Ferries in order to provide adequate numbers of crossings, reasonable rates, and a replacement program for existing vessels?

Mr. Speaker, the matter of adequate ferry service is described by the Hon. Member. The acquisition of new vessels is the subject of a study that has been commissioned by Transport Canada. The study will undertake to look at the various options and the vessel and service requirements that would be necessary to meet needs until the year 2000. I am expecting the report of those recommendations sometime in February. I certainly invite the Hon. Member to provide me with his advice and suggestions on how we might better improve the service.

Mr. Speaker, 1 have a question for the Secretary of State for Canada, who is responsible for the Status of Women. subtopic: ADVISORY COUNCIL ON THE STATUS OF WOMEN

speechtext: January 31, 1985

subtopic: ADVISORY COUNCIL ON THE STATUS OF WOMEN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to assure my colleague, the former chairman, that the matter is within a matter of weeks of being resolved. Minister tell us who is making routine decisions involving the staff? Who runs the Council? Is it the Hon. Minister?

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister for International Trade. knows, what we are presently doing in the discussion paper is examining all options and asking for all points of view. Following that, we will consider whether or not that suggestion would be viable for our trade.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. Here we go again. You are the one who said it.
Let me say that, by removing this obstacle that will inhibit small business from creating more jobs, we will be able to create jobs for many, many more working women.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of State for Tourism. I am sorry that the Attorney General of the Province of Ontario, the Hon. Roy McMurtry, is not here to hear this. It was the most generous of all the agreements signed with any of the provinces, save one. On a per capita basis I think it was, by any standard, a lot of largess from the federal treasury.
Indeed, in the 16 or 17 weeks during which I have been Minister of Tourism, I have signed more agreements with more provinces, worth more money, than the previous Government did in the entire term it was in office.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, 1 have a supplementary. I am sorry I stunned the Hon. Minister, but the word I used was borrowed from one of his provincial colleagues in the Conservative Party.

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Masse that Bill C-20, an Act to amend the Canadian Radiotelevision and Telecommunications Commission Act, the Broadcasting Act and the Radio Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture.

subtopic: CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before one o'clock I was addressing the objectives of Bill C-20 which relate to offering a power of policy direction over the CRTC in broadcasting and in telecommunications matters, to be exercised by Governor in Council, as well as a power to allow Cabinet explicitly to order the CRTC to deregulate telecommunications services that can be provided on a competitive basis.
This power of policy direction in Section 14.1 was recommended by the Lambert Royal Commission as well as by the Special Parliamentary Committee on Regulatory Reform. As part of the March, 1983 broadcasting strategy, the previous Government announced that it would introduce the power in legislation. The power in necessary if the Government is to ensure that its policies are carried out by the CRTC in the areas of telecommunications and broadcasting. Without this power, the Government cannot control the direction of policy development, placing it in an essentially reactive position vis-a-vis the Commission. Interested parties, including the provinces, are generally supportive of the power of policy direction. It allows parties to lobby the Government to establish certain policies as part of the regulatory framework.
I draw to the attention of the House a recent example of the CRTC reacting to public opinion. In fact, it was its first reaction to public opinion in many years. It is noteworthy that that reaction took place in the shadow of this pending Bill. The example relates to the refusal of the CRTC to renew the licence provisions of cable operators vis-a-vis the carriage of a certain FM station, KMBI-FM from Spokane, on cable systems in Calgary and Edmonton, Alberta. Apparently this station was offensive in some way to the CRTC because it purported to carry a Christian message. There was such a flood of public opinion against the heavy-handedness of the CRTC that in fact a reversal of the decision took place and happily the station was restored to those particular cable systems.
The power of policy direction is also a necessary instrument to implement federal-provincial agreements on policy matters. The second power, which is referred to as the power to deregulate, is complementary to the power of direction. Generally speaking, this power is intended to increase competition and decrease regulation in telecommunications services. This power is necessary because under present law the CRTC has
no option but to regulate the activities of companies which fall within the Railway Act definition of a telephone company, even though the companies are planning to offer telecommunications services on a competitive basis, thereby removing any need for CRTC regulation of rates.
The second power would allow the Government to order the CRTC to deregulate telecommunications services which the Government felt should not be regulated because they are offered on a competitive basis. For example, the previous Government announced that it intended to license cellular mobile telephone services under the Radio Act on a competitive basis with two companies competing in each market. However, the Commission felt itself legally bound to regulate the companies, albeit in a relatively light fashion. The power to deregulate would allow the Government to order the CRTC to deregulate these services altogether.
As an alternative to the power to forbear, the CRTC argues that questions of deregulation should be decided by the Commission in the first instance using a new power under the Railway Act. If the Government was not satisfied with the CRTC's decision, it could either vary the decision under Section 64 of the National Transportation Act or repeal the decision, issue a policy direction and require the Commission to hold a second hearing. This approach involves considerable delays. Moreover, it undermines the principle that the Government should be responsible for establishing basic aspects of telecommunications policy.
In summary, it is clear that Clause 1 provides some vitally needed direction for the whole broadcasting industry which has many cultural and technological ramifications today.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-20 to amend legislation governing the CRTC, broadcasting and radio was introduced on December 20, 1984, and it is the outcome of the major reform announced nearly a year ago by Communications Minister Francis Fox.
Two major aspects of this Bill must be mentioned. First, the power of the Governor in Council to issue executory directions to the CRTC on any matter within its jurisdiction. Second, it explains clearly the Canadian Government commitment towards the principle whereby all Canadian men and women are entitled to programs which fully respect the dignity and equality of all individuals. That is in keeping with Section 15 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
That last statement deserves every consideration, but it is so closely linked with the new powers given to the Minister that we will have to remain ever vigilant, and we must warn against any attempt at such manipulation as might detract from the primary objective and lead to failure to give priority to important issues related to human respect and dignity. The best way to explain this is to refer to my previous experience as president of the Advisory Council on the Status of Women.
The issues of dignity, respect and equality which we were talking about concern women particularly, and they are too often related to the problem of violence.
During my term with the Council, that outlook did mobilize our efforts over a number of years. Since 1975, the Council has voiced specific recommendations for major reforms to our statutes and to the administration of justice. Our assumption had been that our statutes should be one of the mirrors of our society. But it has been our experience that such a mirror too often has distorted to a very high degree the actual facts, and it had become urgent to change the glass.
The Council was therefore pleased to see the new direction taken by legislators in amending that part of the Criminal Code which deals with sexual offences, first by deleting and second by reviewing obsolete offences, and stressing the values and mentalities that more truly reflect present day perception of sexual offences.
I would ask you to become aware of and to be heedful of violence against women, and also of violence in general, especially violence against children. Acts of violence against children also point out a frightening reality. All this leads us to ponder over the roots of that evil.
In that respect, the broadcasting of any violence, by whatever means but especially by means of television, which comes under the jurisdiction of the CRTC, disseminates and legitimizes in some way those forms of violence, and their repetition generates senseless and brutish acts of pointless violence.
It is essential that this House should pay attention to and monitor that area, and hopefully the new power given to the Minister in this area will be used with judgment, responsibility and respect for the individuals and groups concerned with
those parameters, and not used to other less honourable purposes, but true to our expectancies. These new provisions and attitudes have become absolutely essential because of the growing pattern of violence. It is also because of women's new open approach to their sexuality that the absolute need for such amendments has been identified. That approach is in turn conditioned by the over-all feminist process. Women's reaction in the face of the kind of violence they are too often still subjected to is not a phenomenon separate from the over-all status of women.
In that context, the Criminal Code's new philosophy with respect to sexual offences answered the legitimate expectations that were based on the concept of violence and put the emphasis on the effects rather than on the nature of the act.
Notwithstanding the principles of equality and respect, the mere fact that in our society thousands upon thousands of women are abused justifies such an intrusion into the privacy of families by means of a better monitoring of the media, those privileged intruders into the life of the private individual and family. Their exemption was no longer justified. In that respect, the Minister is to be commended for recognizing the importance of such reform undertaken by the Liberal Government under the leadership of the then Minister of Communications, Mr. Francis Fox.
A word of caution is needed however. That lofty intention which fulfills specific needs in certain areas as I illustrated earlier, should not open the door to high-handed attempts at promoting specific values that would prejudice the effects of a positive representation of women and other groups. This without infringing upon the freedom of expression provided for in the Broadcasting Act, but always keeping in mind the provisions of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, especially as far as Section 15 is concerned.
Furthermore, the new powers given to the Minister must be implemented with a true political will to safeguard dignity and justice, and not remain pious wishes without direct effective action.
This Government, Mr. Speaker, too often has delighted in utopic promises, aimed only at appeasing certain interests, but where safeguards and action are still forthcoming.
My party, Mr. Speaker, is very much concerned with this reform. We intend to give it constant attention during consideration in committee.
This Government must show its political will but within the spirit of the legislation, which is to prevent and not to serve as a springboard for directed action that would bypass the actual problems with which we are confronted, and important features of which have been described in my speech.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-20 is a modified version of a Bill which was introduced in the last Parliament by the then Minister of Communications. The major difference is that the part of that Bill which dealt with the reorganization of Bell Canada has been separated and the House will deal with that part when Bill C-19 is debated.
Bill C-20 deals with the power of the Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse) to give broad policy directions to the CRTC on matters of important public concern. This Bill also gives the Governor in Council the power to exclude a service or activity from regulation by the CRTC. We support the idea that the Minister should have the power to lay down broad principles. However, we are somewhat concerned about the greater power which the Minister wants. The Minister of Communications has long been able to pass the buck on contentious issues by arguing that they were being considered by the CRTC. At the same time, the Minister has said that he will bring forward a policy on the broad question of telecommunications. We agree that the Minister and the Government should have the power to lay down broad policy guidelines. But, because the Minister has not yet enunciated his policy on telecommunications, and because the CRTC-as it is legally entitled-is still dealing with the question, we have the very strange situation in which the CRTC is now looking into the question of the deregulation of the telephone system. The CRTC is now considering the application of the CNCP Telecommunications system to enter the long-distance telephone service.
It has been argued by Bell Canada-a company for which I have no great love-by consumer organizations, and by the telephone companies of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba-all of which are publicly-owned systems-that to permit CNCP Telecommunications to enter the long-distance telephone business in competition with the existing system, would have a tremendously adverse effect on their systems. It would have a disastrous effect on local subscribers. We have a great telephone system in Canada. It has been estimated that 97 per cent of the people in Canada have telephones. The telephones are modern and efficient, and the rates which Canadians pay for the service are relatively low. Certainly they are low in comparison to the rates which are paid in other countries. A large part of the reason for the telephone rates being so low is that the systems have charged rates for long-distance telephoning which have provided substantial profits. Those profits have been used to subsidize the rates which are paid by home owners, farmers and small business people.
The United States deregulated their telephone system some years ago, and there is evidence that deregulation and the permitting of competition for long-distance rates has driven them down, but has meant very substantial increases, some-
CRTC Act
times in the neighbourhood of 100 per cent to 200 per cent, for local telephone subscribers. That will happen in Canada if the CNCP application or any other application is permitted. That view has been expressed by telephone systems, provincial Governments and consumers groups.
The Minister has said that he will bring forward a policy paper on telecommunications. If that is not done, before we know it the CRTC may indeed make a very fateful decision and give CNCP the right to compete with the existing telephone systems. The losers will be home owners, farmers and small business people. The winners, the people who will get the benefits of competition, will be the large corporations, which have a tremendous volume of long-distance business. So we say to the Minister that if he wants the power to lay down broad policy guidelines, we will support him, but we want him to exercise that power now not later.
There is a section of the Bill which we oppose, and that is Part I, Section 14.6, which gives the Minister the power to exclude services or activities from regulatory control on the basis of competition that is sufficient to ensure just and reasonable rates. This constitutes a broad and unnecessary expansion of the powers of the Minister to deregulate broadcast or telecommunication activities. I understand that the Ontario Government opposed the deregulation of telephone systems before the Government had established the policy.
Part II of the Bill deals with revisions to the Broadcasting Act. First, it clarifies the definition of a broadcasting undertaking to include any person who distributes or transmits a signal other than a telecommunication common carrier whether or not for remuneration. This clarification arises out of the failure of the federal Government in prosecuting unlicensed broadcasters. In 1978 the Government prosecuted the Holiday Inn in Winnipeg and it lost the case. In Part II, clause 3, a new provision, is added to broadcasting policy to prohibit discrimination on the basis of sex. Other changes are consequential to the changes in Part II and Part III.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald), has already indicated the position of our Party with regard to the section dealing with sex. We believe that the addition of this provision is to provide for the promotion of equality and dignity under the Broadcasting Act which arises out of the findings of the special subcommittee on sexually abusive broadcasting. This provision will bring the Act into conformity with the Charter. Therefore, we support the amendment.
We have some concerns, Mr. Speaker, about Part III. We believe it is consistent with Part II which revises the Broadcasting Act and clarifies what constitutes a broadcasting undertaking in the Radio Act. The effect of this, however, will be to require rooftop master antennae on hotels, condominiums and apartment blocks to be considered as TV receiving businesses. Individual households, taverns and small apartment blocks will continue to be exempt. We do not oppose the extension of regulatory control to satellite receiving and

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak today in favour of Bill C-20, an Act to amend the Canadian Radio-Television and Telecommunications Commission Act, the Broadcasting Act and the Radio Act. There are two significant factors to which I would like to address my comments, the first being the amendment to allow Government direction in matters of policy concerning the CRTC, and the second being the Broadcasting Act as it pertains to abusive programming.
First of all, dealing with Section 14.1, in the minds of many Canadians, and I speak both as a former broadcaster and as
CRTC Act
one who has an interest in communications, this provision is long overdue. As we watch the work of the CRTC, we must distinguish in a more clear and forthright fashion the difference between the establishment of policy and the parameters of regulation. Historically, the CRTC, through its regulatory powers under the present Act and through convention, has established what amounts to policy. This particular clause empowers the Governor in Council to issue directions to the commission concerning areas of general policy, for example, the matter of telephone deregulation which has been debated by others today. As one who believes that the policy-maker, the Government of Canada, should be the one to establish the general policy regarding telephone competition-and I think I echo the views of many people-I would like to see the matter of telephone competition under the direction of the Governor in Council. This would include the matter of committee study and the process of consultation.
As a Member of Parliament from Saskatchewan I have risen in this Parliament before to voice my concerns about the proposed deregulation as it would affect Saskatchewan. This is why I prefer the process of consultation with the Minister in the political process to determine what exact policy we as the Government should take in this particular area. It has been well documented in a Saskatchewan study, both by the provincial Government, consumers' organizations and many other people, that the impact of opening up long-distance telephone communications in Saskatchewan would be very debilitating. This is particularly true in rural Saskatchewan where the high cost of installing even basic phone service is offset by SaskTel, the government-owned telephone company, which does so by charging the rates it does for long distance. It is in the interests of the people of Saskatchewan, as it is of people everywhere, for all people to be able to afford a telephone service. I have spoken in this House before on this matter and I welcome the opportunity to be part of that consultative process, so that when the Government gives direction to the CRTC it is done with the national interest in mind. It should acknowledge our differences in the many diverse areas of our province.
Concerning the power of direction, I think it should be stated strongly for the record to those who are concerned about the Government getting directly involved in regulation, or perhaps being seen to be too politically involved, that the amendments clearly spell out under Section 14.1(2) that:
No direction shall be issued ... in respect of the issuance of a broadcasting licence ... the amendment or renewal of a licence ...
The regulatory aspect of broadcast licencing, which should be a matter of the closest regulatory scrutiny, remains under the purview of the CRTC. Further, there is the specific caveat, as we have mentioned, respecting the reference of this matter to committee and opening it to consultation, so it is not and does not appear to be the case of the Government issuing a policy recommendation and thereby being seen to be arbitrary, unilateral or heavy-handed. The approach here is open, conciliatory and consultative.
In looking at the ability of the Government to advise the CRTC on policy, I do have concerns even about the day to day

January 31, 1985
CRTCAct
workings of the CRTC. I acknowledge that this particular proposal deals with national interest and policy. I would like to recount for Members a story of a difficulty that some people in my constituency are having with the day to day functioning of the CRTC. I hope that in the interest of Canadian unity the CRTC will see fit to tighten up its day to day operations. A small cable television company, Battlefords Community Cablevision, is assessed an increase on line rental by the telephone company from time to time. To use the different telephone company lines to carry the cable service, increases are levied as rates go up. Under the regulatory aspects of the CRTC, this company must go to the CRTC and ask permission to pass that increase a long to consumers. It is not a rate increase but merely what is known as a pass through.
The cable company experienced a difficulty some time ago. This year it knew six months in advance when the increase would be effected. It made the appropriate petition to the CRTC to be allowed to pass the increase on to the consumer. The appeal was made in August of 1984. After months of assuring this small cable company that the matter was being addressed, it was only last week that the CRTC got around to putting it into the Canada Gazette. Following the gazetting it will take another month before this proposal can be implemented. For six full months a small cable company has been asking for a very routine procedure.
It is points of day to day operation such as this that concern many Canadians about the CRTC's method of operating. Its bureaucratic method of operating makes small operators and individuals in Canada feel that they cannot deal with this regulatory agency. I hope the CRTC will take upon itself the responsibility to deal in a more understanding and directly responsive way with small cable television operators and small broadcasters in the country.
I would like to discuss the area of abusive broadcasting and the effect of Bill C-20 on Clause 3 of the Broadcasting Act. The provisions in the Bill with respect to abusive broadcasting are welcomed by many Canadians. As one of the members of the Opposition said earlier, this conforms with Section 15 of the Charter of Rights. It is not only a feminine issue per se. The particular amendment reads:
The programming provided by the Canadian broadcasting system should respect and promote the equality and dignity of all individuals, groups or classes of individuals regardless of race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex, age or mental or physical disability;
That provision goes beyond the issues of feminism and deals with the common decency of all Canadians who watch or listen to established broadcasting systems. These people have been demanding a clear-cut standard of what is considered public decency. This is not to undermine in any way the important measures being undertaken by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) regarding pornography in the Criminal Code. This is a matter of taste for many people. Over the years they have seen the standards degenerate to the point of gratuitous violence, sexist stereotyping and very unhealthy role models in terms of derogation of the family on popular television broadcasting. We will now have specifically outlined provisions with regards to abusive programming within the Broadcasting Act.
I found the remarks made in the House this afternoon, particularly by members of the Opposition, to be very interesting. It has been said that this is an old Bill which is simply bringing in something that the past Government brought in. It is significant that in the first six months of the Government's mandate it is acting to effect policy within broadcasting. We are dealing with abusive programming. The last Government took considerably more than six months to listen finally to what Canadians have been saying about the CRTC and to deal with what we have been asking for for a long time with regard to broadcasting in Canada.
It has been said that we should be elucidating a clear-cut policy on telecommunications and deregulation before going ahead with this particular amendment. It is noteworthy that this amendment will go much further than affecting the very important issue of telecommunications and telephone deregulation. It will deal with many other issues related to the wide purview of CRTC in radio, television, telecommunications and other areas. For the sake of the public interest we should move as expeditiously as possible to implement this provision. As we debate specific issues before committee we will have an opportunity to examine further the individual policy initiatives which the Government plans to take.
In conclusion I would like to say that the steps taken in Bill C-20 are only a beginning. Bill C-20 deals with matters other than the specific ones we have addressed such as abusive broadcasting. It deals with matters such as satellite dish rebroadcasting. It lifts a burden off many private broadcasters by extending the maximum license length to seven years from five years. What this Bill endeavours to do could almost be called housekeeping. As we undertake broader policy initiatives and examine further the operation of the CRTC as well as the Broadcasting Act and related Acts and statutes, the Government will be able to embark on a system which more clearly represents the legitimate interests of private broadcasters, cable television operators, small locally owned co-operatives, and distant areas that rely to a greater extent on satellite television. These matters will open up further as we examine the Broadcasting Act and the laws that govern the CRTC.
I would like to indicate my support for this Bill and ask other Members of the House to give it their support. We can study this Bill further in committee. We can now move to the very important job of representing the legitimate interests of Canadians who want a clear-cut policy in the hands of the Government and leave the CRTC to regulate rather than to be the policy-setting agency which in fact it has been.
January 31, 1985

subtopic: CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Essex-Kent is the most southerly riding in Canada. It is the home of Point Pelee Park and Jack Miner's Bird Sanctuary. Wheatley, my town, has the biggest inland freshwater fishery in the world. Furthermore, my riding also includes one of the major communications areas in North America. Those who are familiar with our geography will know that Detroit, Michigan, is located half a mile from the City of Windsor and has been a leading communications centre for many years. However, like many other areas of Canada, it has been affected by CRTC rulings. Station CKLW Windsor, which is a 50,000 watt station, was once the leading radio station in North America. However, as a result of CRTC regulations, it has now dropped to a much lower level. It is an example of how the CRTC does not bend the rules to suit Canadian businessmen.
CRTC Act
In our area it is possible to receive 32 AM stations and 40 FM stations. We can use only rabbit ears to receive 10 to 15 stations. Windsor is one of the last cities in Canada to be cabled. This is being done at the present time.
I spent some 18 months in the broadcasting business, like some of my colleagues. I have seen great changes take place in those 18 years in both private and public broadcasting. I remember when there were only one or two stations available in my rural area of eastern Ontario. Today, television basically runs our lives. It has become the principal disseminator of news, and the principal vehicle for entertainment in the country. It has become the national performance stage and the national forum of information and debate.
It is time for us to decide how we will use these new communications and how they will affect our lives in the future. Canadians now spend half of their leisure time watching television, an average of 23 hours of television per person per week. That is 3.5 hours per day for every man, woman and child in Canada. The combined time that Canadians spend reading books, newspapers and magazines, going to movies, watching VCRs, going to the ballet or symphony, attending a sporting event, playing with the home computer or even doing nothing, does not total the time spent watching television.
I believe it is very appropriate that our Government is introducing new legislation concerning our future and future generations. Our children are spending more and more time watching television and being influenced by television. It is also appropriate that our Conservative Government is changing the Broadcasting Act, because it was during the depression year, in 1932 that the Conservative Party, under the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, established the principle of the national sovereignty of the airwaves and created a national network.
The Canadian Radio Broadcasting Act passed the House with only one dissenting vote. There were only a few radio stations at that time that were low in power and were being overpowered by the United States.
Just 50 years later, communications have changed, but in many ways we still face the same old problem of being inundated by U.S. programming. The numbers of hours of television watched by our children will certainly have an effect on our future generations. What R. B. Bennett said in 1932 still holds true today, that this country must be assured of complete Canadian control of broadcasting from Canadian sources, free from foreign interference or influence.
This is the purpose of Bill C-20. It will set out some overdue rules and regulations. I would not say they are long overdue because the communications industry is moving so rapidly that I do not believe even the Government can make changes fast enough to keep up with the industry. This Bill is an attempt to make changes as quickly as possible. It is important to act now before the industry is completely out of control.
We live in an era when consumers can, by the flick of a switch, receive as many as 100 channels to get as varied information as they desire. While I am sure that everyone

January 31, 1985
CRTCAct
would like to have a satellite dish on their roof, I have a personal belief about their effects on the communications industry. I support the fact that this Bill will establish rules and regulations with respect to the distribution of those dishes. I am pleased that it recognizes that programs from pay-TV channels cannot be distributed through dishes on the roofs of hotels and other establishments.
If consumers believe that everything is free, I suggest that no more programs will be produced because those programs that are now on pay-TV channels are paid for by the cable operators. They buy those films from the producers who, in turn, pay the artists. Consumers must realize that programs that are transmitted through the air are not necessarily free. If these programs are pirated, there will simply be no more programs. Who will pay the artists if no one pays to watch the programs?
I also support the provisions that prevent the owners of apartment buildings from distributing programs to their tenants. If they were allowed to do so it would cause further hardship to cable companies that are already experiencing financial difficulty.
With respect to the control of our broadcasting system, I would be the first to object to the Government dictating what goes on the air. I am sure that if the Government had found it possible, it would have changed some of its policies with respect to cut-backs to the CBC. Some Hon. Members are aware that I had worked for the CBC for 18 years, and some people may also say that I took a roundabout way to avoid being laid off. However, it should be noted that the Government does have an arm's length agreement with the CBC not to interfere with its daily programming. The Government can no more interfere with the CBC's decisions about lay-offs than it can with what Mike Duffy says on the air each evening.
I am pleased to have taken part in this debate. In closing I will say that, I have had experience working in private radio for some time and I believe that a licence period of five years is too short. I support the extension of that period to seven years because it will give radio programmers an opportunity to put their programs into effect.

I am reminded of an editorial cartoon that I saw some years ago. General Motors was having difficulty selling its product because too many cars were being bought from Japanese manufacturers. The planners were studying their vehicles, trying to find why they could not sell enough cars. The sign, in block letters behind them, read, "Build a Better Product". How can we build a better product so that more Canadians will watch more Canadian programs? Could the Hon. Member comment on that?

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his question. He has addressed a difficult question. Yogi Berra once said, "If they won't come out to the ballpark, we can't stop them". I think that the same thinking applies here. We can put the programs on television, but we cannot make people watch them.
I feel we cannot simply sell out to the Americans completely. I have a great fear-if I might diverge from this matter a little-regarding the way the telecommunications industry is going. Again, one cannot legislate morality, in my opinion. But when a person can go to the corner store, buy a movie, go home and watch the movie, and do this continually every night, it bothers me. Are we going to have a generation of people who watch only western movies, if that happens to be their favourite, and what about those who watch a Playboy cassette, or whatever? It bothers me. Is this what we intend to do for our entertainment each night? I feel that as long as we have the commercial networks and the public networks, at least on some occasions some people might tune in to The Journal, an opera on CTV or CBC, or watch The Nature of Things and those types of programs. What happens if we simply throw up our hands and say, "It is wide open, folks. Do whatever you like". I realize that we cannot stop somebody from going home and watching a VCR, if that is his choice. If everybody is watching VCRs, who is going to produce the programs for the CTV, the CBC, Global or other channels? That is a problem and I do not know how we should address it. It certainly will be a problem.

am very happy to see that during the past that was one area left alone by CBC management, and so the 90 minutes of news and information are on each night. I believe it is the only station in Canada doing that. It has been doing it for about a year or a year and half.

the Government has decided to include these matters in another piece of legislation, namely Bill C-19. I am therefore not concerned about the omission of telecommunications in this Bill. My major concern, and what I consider to be an important omission is the fact that this Bill says nothing about the CBC and virtually nothing about the development of the movie industry in Canada, two issues which were amply covered by the previous bill sponsored in this House by the Hon. Francis Fox.
I shall come back to these omissions later, but as I begin my comments, I want to say that this is a matter of some concern for me. One thing that I like however about this bill is the fact that, in what remains of the previous legislation, at least part of the philosophy of the previous Liberal Government has remained. The Government wants to have more power over the CRTC in areas which I believe to be compatible with the arm's length relationship that the government must have with the whole broadcasting system in Canada. What we find objectionable is the interference of the Government in the granting of licences to broadcasters. At the time, the Liberal members of Parliament did not want the Liberal Government to get into this for fear of control over the granting of broadcasting permits. Indeed, this was not one of the changes contained in the previous legislation. In this regard, we note that the Conservative Government is quite right, in not wanting to interfere in the granting of permits, even though I would have no objection if the new powers which the Minister will have and which will allow him to have some influence over certain of the policies of the CRTC, went as far as to enable him to examine the criteria governing the granting of permits, without, however, the Minister or the Governor in Council being able to decide which broadcasting company will obtain a permit. On the other hand, as for the Government having its say in the matter of the criteria impartial selection, it seems to me that it might be a field in which the Government could intervene, on the condition that it will do so with good judgment.
By agreeing to Bill C-20, we shall be giving additional powers to the Governor in Council, and therefore to the Minister of Communications and the Government. I must admit that it is not without some concern that I shall finally give my agreement to this bill. We trusted the former Minister who had always, as did his predecessors, maintained a very clear boundary between the Government and the Broadcasting system in Canada. However, the new Minister of Communications seems to have a tendency to intervene a bit more than his predecessors.
First of all, CBC is completely removed from the jurisdiction of the CRTC. However, it seems that the Minister wants to become himself more involved in the affairs of the CBC. Before introducing Bill C-20, he approved cuts of $75 million in the operating budget of the CBC and of $10 million in the capital budget of that corporation. We are also concerned
when we see the Minister requesting new powers on the broadcasting system in Canada. The Minister has made cuts in the budgets of the NFB and of the National Arts Centre. And today, he is asking for more power to influence the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission. But before he made that request, he slashed $1.5 million in the budget of the CRTC. In addition, the Minister will in some way penalize the broadcasters when the rates set for the applicants of broadcasting licenses will be drastically increased. Indeed, a review of the estimates tabled in the House shows that as a result of those new rates, the CRTC will increase its revenues by a hefty $22 million. The Minister did all that before he even began to consider how he could exert some influence on the CRTC.

There is also something else that concerns me. When the cuts were made and some Canadians were anxious about the effect of those cuts on the quality of programming at the CBC, he eagerly rose and indulged in heroics as he suggested that CBC was not cutting its programming but rather its administration costs. He tried to act as the saviour of programming. The fact was flatly denied by the president of the CBC, Mr. Juneau.
I submit that the arm's length relationship between the government and the broadcasting system in Canada should be maintained. That is why we will keep an eye on the use the government is about to make of the new powers that are being granted by Bill C-20 over the CRTC.
I think that whoever reads Bill C-20 cannot help but notice that there is no mention at all of the first and foremost Canadian broadcaster, namely, the CBC.
We are left to wonder who now is the real boss of the CBC? If the CRTC can no longer issue directions to the CBC, it is therefore the Minister who does! And given the unfortunate way in which the Minister has dealt up to now with the CBC, we have every right to worry and ask questions of this government.
Let us return to the objectives which should determine the government when it gives instructions from now on to the CRTC, since this is what this bill is all about.
In this connection, I submit that the Department of Communications and the Government should aim first and foremost at quality programming.
One of the most deplorable aspects which one can observe in the whole area of broadcasting in Canada is that the goal of quality programming is unfortunately not always compatible with the financial concerns of the producers and broadcasters.
While channel-hopping every night in the quietness of our homes, we realize the wide chasm which exists in the quality of the various broadcasts. There is no mistake that the CBC or Societe Radio-Canada, as it is called in French, is the leader in the area of quality programming in Canada. It is also the leader as far as protecting the Canadian identity. The problem, however, is that the CBC is very expensive and is funded with taxpayers' money. That is something which several Hon. Members have already mentioned and which has resulted in the budgetary cuts which I have indicated earlier. We must realize just the same that quality programming often results in decreased revenues for broadcasters. It brings about lower benefits for shareholders. That is why I suggest that it was wrong to divert the CBC from the influence of the CRTC. And I am anxious to see what sort of relationship the CBC and the Minister of Communications will entertain.
Quality programming must be the first consideration, something which is eagerly sought after throughout our broadcasting system, and the Hon. Member for Nanaimo-Alberni (Mr. Schellenberg) who is a newcomer in this House, was absolutely

right when he compared the quality of American cars to the quality of Japanese cars. We have the same problem with respect to the quality of programming. And that is, for the most part, at the root of our problem of Canadian content.
This is the problem that threatens English-speaking Canada which has the feeling that it is continuously being invaded by American programming. There is first of all the sheer quantity of programs from south of the border. There is also another phenomenon, namely the quality of programs. In larger cities like Toronto and Winnipeg, when looking at the reports compiled by the BBM, the agency that gathers statistics on TV audiences, it is a pitiable sight to see that fairly often the seven or eight favorite programs watched by the local people are American-made. We too have this problem in French Canada, but to a much lesser degree. First of all, French Canada is protected by the language barrier. Yet it is striking to look at the BBM reports and see what the most popular programs are in Montreal, for example. We are also sadly surprised to see that among the four or five most popular programs there are two or three that are American.
So, probably the most important problem facing the CRTC, if they really want to protect Canadian culture and particularly the Canadian culture in English Canada, unprotected by the language barrier, will be that of dealing with the Canadian contents problem and, in the end, the problem of quality. And this is the point where some of the deregulation objectives proposed by the Minister of Communications are beginning to worry us. I think the danger that threatens us with respect to deregulation is most of all one of anarchy in the broadcasting system. Usually coming next is the problem of low revenue, the problem of ensuring a fair sharing of revenue between the broadcasters, which eventually always end up affecting quality.
Mr. Speaker, my remarks will simply make you aware that on this side of the House, while we agree over the broad objective of Bill C-20, we will have to think it over for some time before giving it our approval. I would even go so far as to ask the Minister to rise in the House during the debate on Bill C-20, and make a statement on the way he intends or expects to meet some of the objectives I have mentioned, particularly with regard to the quality of programming and the protection of Canadian culture against the invasion of American programs. I am officially extending that invitation on behalf of my party. We would greatly appreciate it if the Minister, before being granted the nonetheless significant powers he is requesting through Bill C-20, powers enabling him to interfere in the policies of the agency monitoring radio and television in Canada, could make a statement in the House on these objectives and answer questions asked by Opposition members and even by members of his own party anxious to know more about the objectives the Minister will want to pursue when in the future he will have the possibility to influence the CRTC.
