Louis David Riel LOUIS DAVID RIEL

that Bill C-217, an Act to revoke the conviction of Louis David Riel, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I rise today to discuss this Bill in order that a wrong of long ago can be righted. I will be brief in order to give my colleagues in the other two Parties time either to confirm their election promises that they support this measure, or to deny yet another promise to the Metis people by not allowing this Bill to pass.
1 do not seek a pardon for Louis Riel which would, of course, be the purview of Her Majesty and the right of the Crown and, as such, would require a motion seeking permission to receive royal consent as opposed to assent. Instead, Sir, I seek a revocation of the conviction of Louis David Riel. I seek the expression of Parliament's will that this conviction was wrong, that Louis Riel was never guilty of the offence of high treason, and that Parliament now wishes to take the action it should have taken at the time, 100 years ago, to recognize the Metis and other native people's right to selfdetermination and the right to negotiate the terms of their entry into the Canadian confederation.
Louis David Riel, his role in Canadian history, and the long-standing controversy over his execution for treason, have long aroused in many Canadians a profound sense that errors of both commission and omission remain to be addressed and rectified. There is a great sympathy in the public mind for action in the reclamation of Riel's stature as the father of the Confederation we now enjoy and as the founder of the Province of Manitoba, in recognition of the cause Riel fought and died for, a cause with which the people of Canada are only now grappling through the aegis of constitutional discussions on aboriginal rights.
Parliament has a special interest in the Riel legacy because of the dual, often Janus-like, role that this House has played in the events leading up to the execution of Riel and the destiny of Diaspora left to the Metis people in 1870 and again in 1885. This destiny has been further reinforced by federal action again and again ever since. Riel served as the first duly elected Member of this House for the constituency of Provencher. Yet, for reasons intimately tied to his subsequent persecution, he was denied the right to take a seat here and instead was forced into exile. Later, 100 years ago this November, Riel was hanged, not the least of the motives being the unseemly revenge against his actions in 1870. This was the error of commission undertaken by the Government of the day and, until rectified in this House, it is an error shared by every Member of this House.
The fundamental terms of the union, struck by Riel's provisional Government with the Dominion of Canada, as it was then known, despite their legitimate constitutional stature,
have yet to be met. This is a continuing error of omission. Parliament, therefore, has a privileged interest in ensuring that the errors of commission committed against one of its former members, who was so shabbily treated in the early 1870s, so unjustly tried, convicted and hanged in 1885, be redressed.
We cannot revive Riel or compensate for the damage done to his family and to his people, but we can take action to ensure that Canada and Canadians accept that an error was made and that justice, however delayed, is nevertheless done. Parliament has a special obligation to respect the earnestness of the Metis people in their opposition to any measure, such as a pardon, which would merely legitimize the errors of commission and perpetuate the errors of omission.
Today's climate of federal and provincial reticence seriously to respect the need for entrenchment of aboriginal and Metis rights in the Constitution means that we must act to remove barriers to change. We can start by having Parliament say that Louis Riel was innocent of the charges brought against him. This small action in the centennial year of Riel's death is not intended to close the book on this issue but is only the first chapter of our fundamental, and ultimately more pressing, obligation to the Metis people as a whole. That obligation to settle the grievances of land claims and constitutional rights has been waiting 100 years to be settled. If Parliament acts now, we can start down the road to justice, knowing that we have removed some of the unjust actions of our predecessors.
Just as Japanese Canadians seek redress for actions taken by this Parliament in wartime, so too do I seek redress for wrongs done in the aftermath of another war in which Canada extended its sovereignty into another nation's territory, the Metis and Indian lands to the west, and then prosecuted their leaders as being treasonable to the country, a country of which they had never actually agreed to be part. Until all of the treaty rights which were negotiated for and never received and the rights which were taken away without treaty are returned, this issue and the good name of Louis Riel will not be resolved.
I ask this House at a most appropriate time, 100 years since Louis Riel's death, to do something about which we will all be happy, that is, to correct the wrong which was committed 100 years ago.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak to the House today on the motion of the Hon. Member for a number of reasons. First, I want to applaud the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) for bringing this motion before the House. In doing so, he is perhaps making more Canadians aware that this is in fact the one hundred-year anniversary of the rebellion to which he refers. I hope that the results of his motion and the anniversary celebrations which are occurring this year will be more than just a reawakening in the public's mind of the fact that 100 years ago there was a rebellion-in fact, a second rebellion. I hope that Canadians will take the opportunity during the course of this summer to learn more than they now know about the role of the Metis in Canadian history.
January 31, 1985

I am pleased to participate in this debate for personal reasons. I was born and raised in the Province of Saskatchewan in a place not far from Batoche, which will be the scene this summer of the one hundredth anniversary of that final struggle. As you know, Mr. Speaker, I now live in the Province of Manitoba, and Louis Riel was very much the father of Manitoba. There is no debate in history about that particular point. As you may also know, Mr. Speaker, in my previous endeavours I was an historian of western Canada, so that the subject of Louis Riel has been, and continues to be, a subject of great interest to me. In addition to that, I have had the privilege over the years of teaching a number of Metis students at university. I know the importance to them of the subject which is before us.
This is a very timely debate, Mr. Speaker, for two or three reasons. It is timely because this year in fact is the one hundredth anniversary of that rebellion of 1885. The Province of Saskatchewan, from which the Hon. Member comes, has named this Heritage Year in part as an opportunity to commemorate the role of the Metis in the history of that particular province. I might note in passing that I understand that a number of the events which are related to the International Year of Youth will also be directed toward Metis youth in particular.
I believe it is exceedingly important to understand, in my opinion, at least, as an historian and as a politician, that Louis Riel should be remembered for his life rather than his death. The part I regret most about the Hon. Member's motion is that it directs attention primarily to his death and the way in which that event was subsequently handled by historians. Louis Riel should be commemorated for his contribution to Canadian history. He was a distinguished western Canadian in that he was the father of Manitoba. Unfortunately, even as I listened to the Hon. Member, it seemed to me there was some confusion of events between the rebellion of 1869-70, which led my province into Confederation, and the rebellion of 1885, which was an unsuccessful military event and the people whom Riel led were the principal losers in many senses of the word.
The young Riel, the Riel of 1869-70, was a remarkable young man. He had recently returned from his studies for the priesthood in Quebec, studies which he unfortunately never completed because of the untimely death of his father. That had a tremendous impact on him personally. He returned to the Prairies an unemployed person, not unlike many of the young people today who have talent and no opportunity to utilize their talent. He came back to a very agitated society. By 1869 the Red River was undergoing a dramatic socio-economic change. Those of you who are familiar with the history of the West may well remember that Fort Garry in the early part of the 19th century was a fur trading post. It also became a retirement home, if you will, for fur traders who were unemployed after the union of the two principal fur trading companies in 1821. Many people, some from the Orkney Islands and others from eastern Canada, particularly those who were the byproducts of marriages which had taken place according to
Louis David Riel
the country style between fur traders-both of French and Scottish descent-
Order! What has that got to do with the Bill?
It has a great deal to do with the Bill.
It has nothing to do with it.
The purpose of the Bill is to recognize the role of Louis Riel in history.
No, the purpose is to revoke his conviction, you idiot? Read the Bill!

I am suggesting to the Hon. Member, and I think he was not listening, that it is important to recognize and commemorate the life of Louis Riel rather than the death of Louis Riel. There was a very unique culture developing in the Red River area to which Louis Riel came back at age 23 in 1868. He then became a very distinguished leader of the new and growing Red River society.
As a result of the troubles, Mr. Speaker, the people of the River River, not just the Metis but the collective community, united together for the most part in opposition to what they perceived to be the encroachment of central Canada. They were of course acting very much in the tradition of western Canadian history.
As a result of deliberations which took place over several months, the very small postage stamp Province of Manitoba entered into Confederation in 1870. It was very clear that one person more than any other was responsible for that, and that individual was Louis Riel.
As a result of his success he was elected to the House of Commons twice. Regretfully, because of the conflict which existed in Canada in the 1870s-
Called bigotry.

He was barred from taking his seat. The tragedy of Riel in 1870 was that he and many others in that community became a part of a struggle with which they were not in any way involved. This struggle was between the English and the French, the Catholics and the Prostestants. I have talked about this on other occasions at regional meetings of the Metis Federation, and what matters to them is that Louis Riel and his role in Canadian history should be and must be recognized to a much greater degree than it has been up to this point in time. I would hope that our intention during the course of this year will be to commemorate the accomplishments of the entire Metis nation-
Yes, by passing this Bill.

-not to focus simply on one individual. Riel was only a small part of a group of people whose accomplishments in Canadian history were very substantial.
1890

January 31, 1985
Louis David Riel
As I said before, the Metis people were unique in that they were a byproduct of two particular cultures, and they themselves, perhaps more than any other group of people, were responsible for the peaceful settlement of the West. Contrasting Canadian history with American history, we note that our history was much more peaceful, and thankfully so. One of the reasons for that is that the Metis people were a liaison, a vital and continuing link. We have not had in the history of the Canadian West a clash between two cultures which had had no previous contact with or understanding of each other. Riel and the Metis were an integral part of that relationship.
It is extremely important, Mr. Speaker, that Canadians attempt to understand in this centennial year how the history of the Metis is divided into two separate areas, that is, the Metis in Manitoba and the Metis in Saskatchewan. In my mind, the Metis were the victims of technological change.
Like the CPR and the Gatling gun.

Certainly the problems which developed in Manitoba in 1869 were, to a very large degree, a byproduct of the coming of the railway. Unfortunately, after 1870 and the arrival of settlers from southeastern Ontario, many of the Metis left the Red River and went into the North Saskatchewan-South Saskatchewan River area where Batoche is located. Many went into what is now Alberta, your home province, Mr. Speaker. Here they remained, while Riel was out of the country, for 10 or 12 years until the arrival again of the CPR. In the meantime, a tremendous tragedy took place in the Indian community because of the failure of the policies of the Canadian Government to negotiate with respect to reserves. This, the coming of the railways and the coming of the settlers, leads us directly to the crisis of 1884 and the return from Montana of this now not-quite-so-young Louis Riel.
When I look at the events of 1884-85 in the Northwest Territories, I think it is a mistake to think only in terms of one individual. In doing that we are probably doing a disservice to the individual because we are placing too much stress upon the events of 1885 and the results of that particular trial.
It is a service to the Metis people.
In addition to that, we place too much stress on the role of one individual in the history of an entire culture.
Nonsense!
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend is entitled to his opinion. He has had his few moments, and I think I am entitled to mine.
You have had your few moments.

In 1884-85, the Canadian Government was guilty, as it has been so often throughout our history, of neglect. There was a breakdown in communications. Every western Canadian knows the story of letters being sent
to Ottawa and answers coming back weeks and months later. Unfortunately, that is a problem which does not always seem to be restricted to the 19th century. There was a recession on the Prairies and cut-backs in the Department of Indian Affairs. By 1884, the climate on the Prairies was explosive. The Canadian Government must accept responsibility for that, at least in the sense that this lack of communication had led to its creation.
When Louis Riel returned to Batoche, then deemed to be the headquarters of the Metis community, he returned to a situation to which in part the Canadian Government had contributed. What happened thereafter is a tragedy in that it was a clash between two totally unequal technological forces. On the one hand, you had the so-called modern army from eastern Canada armed with the Gatling gun which had been sent here by the Americans as an experiment. On the other hand, there was an aging and weaker society in the Metis culture trying to defend itself against new methods of warfare. In my opinion, the Metis people would have been better off had the second rebellion not occurred. The rebellion occurred, and I think that in many ways the Metis people were the victims of that for the reason that their history had been tied almost exclusively to one individual, the figure of Louis Riel.
In this particular case it is important to look back and recognize that the history of a people is more than the history of one individual. It is also important to realize that one can be heroic and still have controversial characteristics. As an example I think of John A. MacDonald, the first Prime Minister of Canada. Teachers of Canadian history were embarrassed for many decades to admit that the man had certain problems with alcohol consumption. Later on we became mature enough to realize that the man was heroic despite his weaknesses.
I am saying that the Metis people can and should be proud of their accomplishments regardless of the controversial question of how Louis Riel was treated in the judicial courts in 1885. The Metis people should honour Louis Riel for his accomplishments, as should all Canadians, regardless of how the courts dealt with him in 1885.
I read the transcripts of 1885. I dare say there are not many people among the 282 Members who can say that. I do not pretend to be a lawyer; I am only a historian. Having read virtually all of the material that has been published, I can say that the debate on the validity of the trial of 1885 will go on for time immemorial. The fact remains that Louis Riel was an exceptional politician. He was a man of substantial stature who led the people of Manitoba into Confederation. He was very sincere in his attempts in 1885 to get a better deal for the people of the Northwest Territories. It is also evident, and must not be forgotten, that he was part of a people who have every right to be proud of their history and their accomplishments.
January 31, 1985

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be taking part in the debate this afternoon. It is a rather emotional subject, because to us, Louis Riel is a hero. I therefore wish to start by congratulating the Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) for proposing Bill C-217, an Act to revoke the conviction of Louis David Riel.
The explanatory note, Mr. Speaker, reads as follows:
The purpose of this Bill is to revoke the conviction of Louis David Riel for high treason, as opposed to merely granting him a posthumous pardon.
Mr. Speaker, the Member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Clark) spoke as a historian. He made the point that the history of Canada, at least where it concerns the development of this country, is a controversial one and always will be, I imagine, according to the historian himself, a subject of debate. I agree that when we read all the documents on the historic trial and hanging of Louis Riel, there are diverging views on both sides. The fact remains that to many of us, this controversial figure in the history of our country is a hero, a man who managed to unite his people in a common cause and who left his mark on our history, not only as far as his own people were concerned but also, and I think the historian who spoke before me, the Member for Brandon-Souris, will agree, as the founder of the Province of Manitoba.
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to take up too much of the House's time, and I just want to make a few brief comments and invite my Quebec colleagues, as French-speaking Canadians, to take part in this debate and express their views. In every new session, over the last twelve years, we have had occasion to discuss this matter.
The same Bill has been proposed many times before by Members of the New Democratic Party. I heard Mr. Yurko, the former Member for Edmonton East, make the same proposal. There have been many statements under S.O. 43. However, I must admit I have rarely heard any statements or views on the subject by Members from Quebec. I speak today as an Ontarian by birth, with a solid Irish, Scotch and French background, and I would ask those Members in this House who are from Quebec to take part in the debate so that we will finally know where they stand and what their position is on an issue that has been a very important one in this country. The House will remember that Ontario was the bad guy and that Quebec was "deeply offended" by what happened, which gave rise to some serious problems with respect to Canadian unity.
I think this will be an opportunity for our Quebec Members ... I see the Member for Gatineau (Mrs. Mailly) who often speaks during the hour for private Members, and I wonder whether she would be willing to state her views on this important matter. I am sure she is well up on the subject and would be able to give us some clarification regarding the views of those Quebec Members who all too often remain silent on such important issues.
Louis David Riel
Mr. Speaker, to avoid prolonging the debate, to give these Members a chance to express their views, and to show that this House is interested in making some progress in clearing up controversial matters, I would like to make a proposal I consider important. I want to suggest to the Hon. Member who presented the Bill that he withdraw it so it can be referred to committee for consideration. Perhaps the Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) will agree that the proposed legislation deserves more thorough consideration than can be given in one hour here in the House. I therefore move, seconded by the Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) that the motion be amended by deleting all the words following the word "That" and substituting the following therefor:
Bill C-217, an Act to revoke the conviction of Louis David Riel, be not now read a second time but that the Order be discharged, the Bill withdrawn and the subject matter there referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
Mr. Speaker, that is my proposal!

Yes.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak to Private Members' Bill C-217. First I want to express some regret about the speech made by the Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) who, as did the Liberal Party even before 1900, attempted to frame the issue on the basis of whether one is French or English. He tried to put it into a French-English ratio basis. That was incorrect then and it is incorrect today. It is typical of the Liberal Party that it is prepared to play on the deepest emotions that people have had historically in this and other countries for the benefit of his Party.
Having said that, I believe that he does have the correct approach in that this subject matter should be put before a committee. The Bill, as reflected in the scholarship of the Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin), shows the typical simplistic approach taken by the NDP which is lacking in any true appreciation of what the reality was then or what it is now. If there is anybody who is in left field, it is clearly the NDP, ideologically and in reality.

January 31, 1985
Louis David Riel
This topic needs time. With every passing year and with the excellent scholarship by our historians, more is being revealed about the true reality of the situation in Canada at the time. Therefore, I submit that it would be quite improper for the House to act precipitously on this issue by passing this Bill. The amendment by the Member for Ottawa-Vanier is closer to addressing the issue. That may be the proper approach once proper discussions are held and the background set up. Indeed, there are many of us who would be prepared to see that happen in the future.
There is enough scholarship today to allow a committee to get to the bottom of the whole question. In fact, the real issue was a religious issue, which we find very hard to believe today. However, in those days to be a Roman Catholic or Protestant was similar to the situation in Northern Ireland today.
Members of Parliament hold the great privilege of having immunity in this place. I suggest that Members do a disservice to the people of their riding and of the country by trying to take advantage of those deep emotions of people.
The historic truths are jsut now coming to light. The most recent book entitled Prairie Fires written by Professors Bob Beal and Rod MacLeod sets out the context as best as has been done. I do not believe there are any more documents coming to light. Therefore, I believe this would be an appropriate time for the topic to be considered. I hope all Members will read that book because it will give a sense of the background and the reality from which western Members come. When we stand to present our western grievances in the House, as our colleagues from other provinces present their grievances, we must learn more about our historical development.
Members who study this issue will have a deep sense of outrage about what occurred to the Metis people and to Louis Riel. It is true that the actual legal events that occurred were very likely correct and clearly appreciated by Louis Riel himself. He was defended by the leading defence counsel of the nation. There is no doubt that he understood the legal position he was in and the stand taken by the defence counsel on his behalf. They knew in terms of the law that there was only one defence that would prevail for him, but he rejected that defence, quite properly.
The life of Louis Riel shows and the book reveals that by 1869 the Metis people were a totally self-contained racial group in this country. They were not Indians, even though they could live like the Indians in many respects. They were not like Anglophone Canadians, even though they could operate in that world. Indeed there were many English-speaking Metis, although their definition correctly applies only to a French-Indian combination. They were not French Canadians in the tradition of the French habitants and the people who spent their lives in Quebec.
It is not possible to become a separate nation overnight. The Metis had 200 years' experience of being their own people on their own land with their own culture. They lived along the rivers in Manitoba on lots that were surveyed in long lines, as was done in Quebec. Naturally, they objected when surveyors came in 1869 and rejected those property rights in favour of
the square toroid system in which the western country was surveyed. In fact, that is why Louis Riel is a hero to anyone who knows his western Canadian history. Louis Riel was the first man to stand up to the oppressive, unilateral and dictatorial actions of the central Government, and others have subsequently and paid a bitter price for it.
That is what the National Energy Program involved. It reflected an insensitive, uncaring central Government foisting its view upon a region of this country. The National Energy Program was a western Canadian issue, but there could be other measures affecting other provinces. Indeed, Parliament responded in many ways to the pressures that came from Quebec to allow Quebecers who wanted to participate in this country with their language as Canadians. That is what the official language is about. That is why I can defend the Official languages Act in my riding with no problem at all. Its purpose is to allow people who live in a region of our country to feel that they are a part of Canada and can contribute to the greatness of this country.
By the same token, Quebec Members-especially Progressive Conservative Members from Quebec-went to Quebec and argued against the National Energy Program that was so vicious and wrong for western Canadians.
The Provisional Government of Louis Riel was legal. In 1869 and 1870 there was a gap between the time when the central Government got Rupert's Land and the time when the Northwest Territories and its government was legally installed. Therefore, the Provincial Government of Louis Riel was quite correct in terms of law. However, it made a political mistake when it executed Thomas Scott. That inflamed the religious passions, which we find hard to appreciate today but which were very real at that time. That enraged Ontario, just as Quebec was enraged after the execution of Louis Riel. These events were framed in terms of race and religion and they set off an uncontrollable reaction. It inevitably led to the events of 1885.
Again, the Hon. Member for Regina West has made no distinction in terms of his scholarship and understanding of the problem that it is necessary to isolate the events of 1885, which led to the treason charge, conviction and hanging, from the events of 1869. In 1885, Mr. Speaker, it was much the same. Again, the Metis had resettled along the south branch of the Saskatchewan River. They had been there for many years; their children had been born and raised there. They had grandparents and parents who were on the land. That gave them a validity that only farm people perhaps can appreciate, having ancestors who have worked the land and are part of the land. Again, the surveyors came. You would have thought that the central Government by then would have appreciated that one should give respect to some of the rights of the Metis, but the surveyors did not. They simply came and started to trample over their land once more. The Metis did not know what to do. They did not have any natural-born leaders in terms of politics. Gabriel Dumont, the greatest buffalo hunter and organizer they had sent to Montana for Louis Riel. A delegation was sent. Riel came back reluctantly. By that time

he was an American citizen and was proud to be an American. He said he really wanted to remain an American and planned to go back, but the Metis needed his advice. Riel came. They had all sorts of meetings all over the Metis territory. They sent petitions. They wrote out their grievances very carefully, sent them to Ottawa, but Ottawa did not respond. It so happens that the Government was a Progressive Conservative Government. We all express regret that the Government in Ottawa at that time was no better than subsequent Governments have been, the last example being the Liberal Government and the National Energy Program.
The Metis became desperate. At the same time the research shows that in two areas Louis Riel was unable to keep his common sense, as we would say today. One was in politics. He was incensed about what had happened in 1869. He created Manitoba. He got no reward nor acknowledgement. In 1885, he came back. After weeks and weeks they sent petitions and letters, but got no response. Suddenly, troops were sent out. In the area of politics Riel was so frustrated that, again, he took politics into his own hands and declared a separate Government. That was all right in 1869 because in terms of the law there was a gap, and so it was quite acceptable. In 1885, there was a properly, duly constituted law in the Northwest Territories. What Riel did was simply illegal. It was treason to declare it. Then things got out of control, Mr. Speaker. If I recall, 29 or 30 people were killed. These were proper, law-abiding residents who were living in the Northwest Territories and who were killed by the Metis and the Indians. It was out of that that the charge of treason arose.
When it came time for the trial, there was no doubt in terms of the law, with 30 people having been killed, that there was going to be a conviction. Riel's lawyers raised a defence of insanity. Louis Riel himself would not accept that defence of insanity, even though subsequent scholarly studies show that in the area of politics and in the area of religion Louis Riel lost his common sense. In terms of religion, Louis Riel by that time had come to see himself as a prophet. In fact, the leadership of the church at that time was very upset with the position he was taking and developing. Riel wanted to make one of the bishops Pope of the new world and he was going to be the prophet. That is the historic reality of it. The leaders of the church were not happy with him then.
He was hanged.

I say read the letters of Father Andre. Get in and actually do the research. If you want to look at it, it is there in black and white. Therefore, the church leaders, we have to accept, were not all that unhappy. They did not want him to be killed. The irony, I suppose, is that once he was killed and no longer a threat to the leadership, they took Riel to their hearts.

What an explanation!
Louis David Riel

That is the reality, my friend, and I say to you to take a look at it.
This is why this Bill has to go to a committee at some point. If the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier had done his research, he may have come up with that.

Member for Ottawa-Vanier. It is a subject that could be looked at, although I believe it will be found that the conviction of Louis Riel was correct in terms of the common law at that time. Mr. Speaker, I am pleased as a Quebecer to rise today and speak on such an important and interesting chapter of our Canadian history. I would like to join my colleagues from Brandon-Souris (Mr. Clark) and Lethbridge (Mr. Thacker) in paying tribute to a hero of our Canadian history. I consider it important that in this House, occasionally, we should have an opportunity to pay our respects to those men who paid so dearly to have their mark left on our history. I hope that my colleague from Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme) will take part in the debate today. 1 want to point out to the House that we have among us a Metis, and I hope he will contribute to this debate.
Mr. Speaker, it is interesting that such a subject should have been introduced in this House because in this year 1985 the Metis resistance will be commemorated in Saskatchewan and Manitoba. I think it is with much pride that the Canadian Government is now discussing with representatives of the National Council of Metis this matter of grants for the celebration of the 100th anniversary of Batoche, which will take place in Saskatchewan in July of 1985. I must also stress the active participation of the Saskatchewan Government in those activities. The many events that will take place next summer, that is in July 1985, will have the scope of a truly national celebration, with many social and cultural activities, and we are proud as the federal Government to be associated with that event. This goes to prove, Mr. Speaker, that this Government wants to encourage cultural Metis activities in Canada.
We all know here, in this House, that Louis Riel has played a very important role in our Canadian history. We may even think that Louis Riel is one of the founders of Manitoba, even though there has been a lengthy controversy on that subject. We recognize today the important contribution of all the Metis of the area in the building of our Canadian society. The Government of Canada is negotiating with the representatives of the National Council of Metis and other native groups to better define their constitutional role. Besides, I would like to point out to the House that there will be an important conference of First Ministers on April 2 and 3,1985 on the subject of
natives.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, in order not to take up too much of the time of the House, I would like to conclude by expressing my feeling of fraternity with those people who want to be identified in Canada's great mosaic.

Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief, because I know that everyone would welcome the opportunity to vote on the subject. If the Hon. Member who has just spoken truly believes in and wants to make all Canadians aware of the history of the Metis people, I think a first step would be to revoke the verdict of guilty as his Government is empowered to do. I would therefore urge all other members to support us in the Liberal Party with our amendment, to support our friend from the New Democratic Party on his Bill, and stop talking nonsense if you are not ready to vote.

Mr. Speaker, I rise in the House today to speak on this Bill with great emotion because I stand here with a heritage which goes back to the Metis in the Province of Manitoba. In my grandfather's living-room there was a picture of Riel, but it was not the Riel who is being projected here today through this Private Member's Bill. It was the Riel who accomplished something for his people, my relatives.
As I stand here today I look at the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme) and the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier). I have seen them before speaking on issues, presenting Private Members' Bills and trying to create divisiveness within the House.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. This is not the first time the Hon. Member has tried to do that to me. I ask him to tell me when I have ever tried to do such a thing. I have been a Member of this House for 21
years.

Obviously, Mr. Speaker-
It is a negation of what I came here for, what you are trying to do.

-if the shoe fits, wear it. I think the intent of the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) is honourable. I do not question that. However, I think it is slightly misguided, and I hope that it is not for political reasons that he has brought this Bill forward.

Let us look at the Metis accomplishments rather than the eventual problems and outcome which Riel had to face. Let us speak of the accomplishments and contributions they made to the Canadian culture and to the Canadian mosaic. The Hon. Member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Clark) said: "Let's not talk of the death of Riel, but let's talk of his accomplishments, accomplishments which shaped and moulded the lives of many of us Manitobans as we grew up".
From 1869 to 1870, as history proves, Manitoba went through considerable turmoil. There were problems. I say in retrospect that if we had to face those problems today, we would not necessarily have handled them as they were handled then. However, it is part of our history and it is something from which we should learn rather than cause division on.
Riel, in 1869 and 1870, was working and trying to establish a better life for the people he represented. Those people supported him to the point where Mr. Riel had to leave the Province of Manitoba. The Metis did not leave; there are still an awful lot of them there. Some of us have moved on to different areas of this great country, but we contributed and Riel contributed.
I want to tell the House something about growing up in the Province of Manitoba in the era in which I grew up. There were still injustices being done to us. However, we do not look back on them with anger. We have learned. We have learned to be tolerant and to understand. Hopefully, we can pass this on to future generations so that as Canadians we can live and develop a country with understanding for all cultures; not only native Indians and Metis but all cultures which came from all parts of the world to this great country. They knew that there was understanding and that possibly life had to be given to create this great country of ours. Let us look at it positively. Let us not try to divide.
Let's vote now, then.
Let's vote on it.

Let us work toward the future of Canada instead of looking backward.

There is no way in this world that we can make up for the mistakes and wrongdoings of the past. We must seek and continually work toward doing justice within our own time. I have no time for those who would promote divisiveness by the use of this House or by the use of any means or methods within the country.
Hear, hear!

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-AMOUNT OF FARM DEBT. (B) UNITED STATES PROGRAM
AGRICULTURE-AMOUNT OF FARM DEBT. (B) UNITED STATES PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak on the adjournment motion this afternoon because in the gallery today are representatives of the Ontario Federation of Agriculture. Over 150 visited Parliament Hill today and presented a brief to many Members of Parliament, I believe to almost every Member from the Province of Ontario. I welcome them to the Hill today.
Yesterday I directed a question to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) concerning the farm debt crisis, the most important problem presented to us today by the Ontario Federation of Agriculture. They pointed out that almost 39,000 out of 228,000 farmers in Canada face very serious debt problems. This is due to the fact that commodity prices have been very low, interests rates for the past three or four years have been very high and in many cases land values have dropped by at least 50 per cent in the last three or four years. This has resulted in excellent farmers suddenly having no equity in their farm property.

January 31, 1985
Adjournment Debate
An OFA representative who visited my office today described how he had purchased a farm for $320,000 about 10 years ago. He took out a $240,000 mortgage with the Farm Credit Corporation. When he had the farm appraised last summer, the value of his hog farm had dropped to $165,000. He has totally lost his equity in the property due to falling land values.
I asked the Minister what he was going to do about the serious financial difficulties of the thousands of farmers on the verge of bankcruptcy or default. The Farm Credit Corporation estimates that defaults on farm properties in the next couple of years will amount to $2 billion, the largest default since the 1930s. It will be in the realm of Dome Petroleum and other massive defaults in this country. Instead of involving a big oil corporation, it will affect hundreds of thousands of small farmers. What is sad is that these are our youngest and most productive farmers. They are technologically advanced farmers who produce half of all the food produced in this country.
The Minister stated that they had reduced interest rates to 12% per cent. The Farmers Union and the Canadian Cattlemen's Association are asking that the interest rate be reduced to 8 per cent. The Minister said they can appeal to the Farm Credit Corporation in the event of a foreclosure. He said they are running a pilot project to consider ways to assist these farmers.
That policy of the Mulroney Tory Government is a policy of abandonment. They are saying to the 39,000 farmers in serious financial trouble, and the Farm Credit Corporation estimates that the number has grown to 45,000 in the last two months, that they are abandoning them.
Compare that with the policy in the United States. Approximately four weeks ago a number of parliamentarians went to the United States and met the Secretary of Agriculture John Block. He told us that theirs is a policy of continuing to spread the loans over a longer period of time. Two of us had the opportunity to meet and talk with the Farmers Home Administration. We were told that their policy was a policy of continuation and that they wanted to continue to have young, productive and technologically-advanced farmers on the land. They told us that if those farmers were put off the land, the land values would fall on surrounding farms and the situation would be exacerbated.
Let us consider the abandonment policy of the Minister of Agriculture and compare it with the policy of the United States Government. The U.S. is prepared to write down interest rates of from 11 per cent or 12 per cent to 5 per cent or 7 per cent. The U.S. Government is willing to set aside 25 per cent of Farmer's Home Administration loans for a five-year period and is willing to pay the interest on the loans during that period of time. If a private-sector loan is involved, and the bank is willing to forgive more than 10 per cent of that loan, then the Farmer's Home Administration in Washington will provide a loan guarantee for 90 per cent of the balance.
To this date, that administration has had 109 applications. It has processed 3,000 set-aside applications. It has written down 8,000 loans to 5 per cent or 7 per cent. That is the policy which keeps young people on the farms. That is the policy of continuation which strengthens, encourages and supports the rural area.
That is exactly what the Ontario Federation of Agriculture wants this Government to do. However, instead we have the Tory policy of abandonment. The Government has said to the 45,000 young farmers across Canada, "We are abandoning you and the devil take the hindmost. We are not going to support you. We are not going to assist you in any way". It is a callous, uncaring, short-sighted and inhuman way to treat the young farmers who are the life-blood of the rural area and the agricultural economy for the years ahead.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre Blais (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am always somewhat surprised that the Hon. Member for Algoma should constantly raise these questions, which makes us wonder what was the former Government doing when the interest rates were around 16 and 17 per cent. It was this Government which authorized such loans to farmers by the Federation, Mr. Speaker. What we are doing now is to try to minimize the effects of a policy which caused serious problems and was hardly acceptable to Canadian farm producers.
Mr. Speaker, the Member opposite would like to know what action the Government intends to take to prevent farm bankruptcies in Canada. This is what he asked in his question yesterday and today and this is what he spoke about in his comments. 1 would like to point out that, since it came into power, the Progressive Conservative Government has done a lot to prevent these bankruptcies.
During the last few weeks, we have taken several initiatives which will be of great assistance to Canadian farmers. Something over two weeks ago, on January 15, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) announced that 5,600 farmers would be eligible for a reduction in the interest rate on their loan. Many farmers on the verge to bankruptcy now have better hope to overcome their difficulties. Thanks to the action taken by our Government, eligible farmers will be able to save about $16 million a year during the next five years.
To help those who find themselves in a dire straits or against whom legal proceedings have been or will soon be taken, the Government has extended the terms of reference of the appeals commissions of the Farm Credit Corporation. This means that, when a farmer who has borrowed from the Corporation finds himself in dire straits, he will be able to go before these appeals commissions and ask for a review of his case.
He can appear alone or accompanied by his other creditors so that those concerned can look for valid solutions. It is not always easy, Mr. Speaker, but I believe that, as parliamentarians, we must try to find solutions with farm producers instead
January 31, 1985

of simply saying that our policy, is to give up which is certainly not the case. The facts are very clear and I think that the action taken by the Canadian Government since September 4 show a real desire to help farm producers.
Hon. Members have also asked about a debt forgiveness program. We are now considering many options which could help to prevent farm bankruptcies, and I must say that these include such a program.
We have the duty to examine carefully all possible options. A program of debt forgiveness may seem interesting and simple, but we have to consider all its consequences. Subsidizing interest rates could have about the same net effect for the farmer, but it might be simpler to apply. The Government can no longer afford to spend or to reduce its revenue without the assurance that the results will be worthwhile. You can be certain, Mr. Speaker, that the Government will discharge its responsibilities.

subtopic: EDUCATION-FUNDING OF STUDENT LOANS PROGRAM. (B) TUITION FEES QUERY
EDUCATION-FUNDING OF STUDENT LOANS PROGRAM. (B) TUITION FEES QUERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in December I asked the Hon. Secretary of State (Mr. McLean) a very important question regarding his Government's approach to the young people of this country and the availability, access and opportunity for them to have a college or university education, a post-secondary education. 1 asked this question because of the cuts made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in his economic statement in the fall, and because of my grave concern for the future of the young people of this country. I am sorry to say that I did not receive a clear answer, or even an understandable one, from the Minister.
The future of Canada and the future of our young people are inextricably tied. If our youth are properly trained and educated to face the future, Canada will be the beneficiary. If our young people gain the required education, if they are given the opportunity to get an education, they will then, through their imagination and intelligence, be stimulated to think, invent, research, produce and to make Canada's economy much healthier. Not only will our economy be healthier, Mr. Speaker, but also our entire civilization. Its culture, values and quality of life will be enhanced by exposing our youth to a post-secondary education. Therefore, much of our future is in the hands of our youth. If we are to be competitive in the future, we must have a well educated population. We must give access to a post-secondary education to as many young people as possible.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, at this time of high youth unemployment, many of our young people who cannot get jobs are staying in school because they know that statistics prove that the higher the education, the better the chance to get a job. For example, approximately 96 per cent of the people with university degrees obtained jobs last year while nearly 14 per
Adjournment Debate
cent of high school drop-outs were not able to obtain employment.
Professor David Foot, professor of economics at the University of Toronto, who is an expert renowned in his field, has made extensive labour-market studies and has given us ample evidence that education is fundamental to providing a worthwhile future, a future with decent and relevant employment for our young people, and is also vital to the future of our great country and its economy.
With all of the evidence of the importance of post-secondary education to our young people, to our economy and to our healthy future, what does the Tory Government do? It puts a freeze on student loans, holding them to present levels. It takes away the indexed adjustment for the cost of living which was earmarked for students by the former Liberal Government. This it does while hypocritically talking about its concern for those in greatest need. The Tory Government socks it to the student who can no longer afford to stay in school because of the freeze it has put on the level of student loans. The Tories say one thing and do another.
Even in the January, 1985 consultation paper just released this week, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), said, "Social responsibility dictates that wherever possible, and to a greater extent than is the case today, scarce resources should be diverted to those in the greatest need . Is this how the Government diverts resources to those in need? The Tories are quite willing to hurt the poorest kids in our society by removing their ability to borrow important dollars which could make the difference as to whether or not they can attend school. Actions speak louder than words.
It is the student from a family living in poverty, with its limited income, where every dollar counts, who is the one who needs to borrow this money. Not every student needs to borrow the entire limited amount available under the Student Loans Program. They can manage with a partial loan and, fortunately, many can get on without any loan at all. But a ceiling on student loans does hurt the poorest students, those with the greatest need. How could the Conservative Government so cruelly remove the $5 million cost of living increase and hit the students who are weakest and least able to cope, all the while crying crocodile tears about its concern for the poor?
The present Conservative Secretary of State has been given by Parliament the authority to enlarge student loans. He could have increased the loan limits. As a matter of fact, he did not even have to do that. The former Liberal Government had already taken steps to include the increase in its Budget. So why did the Secretary of State freeze them? Why did he sock it to the poor kids in this way?
Maybe the Minister of Finance kept the Secretary of State from doing what I am sure his own conscience told him he should have done. Or did he really want to disenfranchise a whole segment of the student population, the poorest, from their right to a post-secondary education. The students of Canada and the people of Canada are entitled to a clear

Adjournment Debate
answer to this question. Is this Government going to help the poor or just talk about it? How can he possibly justify a freeze on student loans?

Mr. Speaker, in light of the remarks made by the Hon. Member for Eglinton-Lawrence concerning the Government's decision not to raise the weekly loan limit under the Student Loan Program in 1985-86, perhaps I should begin by explaining how this program works.
From the outset, may I point out to the Hon. Member that we are talking about the Canadian Student Loans Program which is administered by the provinces under the appropriate legislation. Student assistance offices in the various provinces analyse the financial needs of applicants, and any loan made under the program take into account expenses incurred by the student for personal needs, his resources and real tuition fees. Therefore, should a province decide to raise tuition fees, as Ontario is about to do, according to the Hon. Member, that factor will be included in figuring out loans. The Hon. Member must know that real tuition fees have always been and will always be taken into account in figuring out loans under the Canadian Student Loans Program. The Hon. Member probably knows as well that in most provinces this program is only one aspect of student assistance; they can also apply for grants or special assistance, or resort to loan programs for additional financial assistance. Taken as a whole, those programs offer generous help.
As to the loan limit at current levels and the reduced outlays for 1985-86, I should tell the Hon. Member that, contrary to what he seems to imply, next year's budget for the Canada Student Loans Program will be increased, from $229 to $270 million. I am sorry to say that we had to cut expenses under this program by some $5 million in 1985-86, but the fact remains that the increase for next year amounts to 17.9 per cent. I am sure the Hon. Member will agree with me that nobody gets any less than what he or she can rightfully expect.
Most students will not be unduly alarmed if the loan limit is frozen at current levels, that is $105 a week. Mr. Speaker, I must point out that a student entitled to the maximum amount can receive $3,360 over a 32-week school year, not to mention any help he might get from the province. The average loan under the program is $2,300, so that the current $105 limit does appear reasonable, but the freeze on the weekly limit might adversely affect the odd student who is otherwise eligible for the full loan. Still, that is $160 a year at most and, keeping in mind the low inflation rate, we do not expect dire consequences.

Mr. Speaker, on November 19, 1984, which seems like a long time ago now, I addressed a two-part question on VIA Rail to the Minister of State for Transport (Mr. Bouchard). The first part had to do with whether VIA Rail had any plans for improving and expanding its service. The second part had to do with what plans VIA Rail had for getting its horrendous deficit under control.
The first part of my question came about as a result of the fact that just prior to the date of my question the Canadian Transport Commission had released a report indicating that of all of the passenger railroads in the industrialized world, VIA Rail had the most obsolete, oldest and worst equipment. That report also indicated that VIA Rail had lost something like one million potential passengers between 1982 and 1983.
The second part of my question dealing with the deficit of VIA Rail was prompted by the fact that in spite of the $93 million reduction in the budget of VIA Rail that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) called for at the beginning of November, VIA was left with a $600 million deficit for the current year. This of course will have to be subsidized by the taxpayers and will be part of that over-all $37 billion deficit which the country is facing right now. If the figures are correct, in 1983 the Government and the taxpayers of the country were forced to subsidize every single passenger on VIA Rail to the extent of $70.
Since November 19 the Government made two announcements; the first was actually made that same evening. On November 19 the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski), speaking in Edmonton, appointed a three-member rail passenger action force. He indicated that the Government had plans to improve and renew the locomotives and equipment of VIA Rail and that the Government was also considering expanding and bringing back some of the passenger lines that had been discontinued by the previous Government. On January 15 of this year the Government announced that it was bringing back six of those discontinued passenger rail lines and reinstating them.
Those are excellent moves, Mr. Speaker, which I think that we all applaud, as far as they go. Unfortunately, I do not think they really address the key question of the $600 million deficit of VIA Rail which is hanging over the heads of the taxpayers of the country. Something must be done about that. One answer is to reduce costs. I am sure we would all applaud that solution. However, that alone is not going to solve a $600 million deficit. The only thing which will overcome that will be to increase the revenue of VIA Rail, and the only way to increase the revenue is to increase the number of passengers who are using the VIA Rail system.

How are we going to increase the ridership on VIA Rail? First, we are going to have to provide faster and more comfortable trains. We must also ensure that those trains leave and arrive on time. The speed and comfort of the trains should be addressed through the new equipment. The question of punctuality is an entirely different matter.
I recently went to meet my daughter at the Union Station in Toronto. She was travelling on a VIA Rail Rapido train coming from Montreal, supposedly arriving at 10.20 p.m. In fact, it did not arrive until 11:15 p.m., almost an hour later than scheduled and after four different announcements of time delays and postponements. One can imagine the feeling of my daughter and the other passengers on the train, and the feelings of myself and those waiting to greet the passengers on that train.
How do we overcome this problem? In my opinion it can be solved in the same way the Americans solved their problem; with an agreement similar to the Amtrac agreement. It is an exclusive right-of-way agreement that provides penalties for the railways over which Amtrac trains travel. We need something similar to that in this country. We must ensure that VIA can provide on-time service.
I would ask the Minister's representatives what plans the Government has to either reach an agreement with CN and CP or to legislate an agreement which will compel an exclusive right-of-way for VIA and ensure that penalties are imposed for interferences and delays with VIA Rail on-time service.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport, I am pleased to answer the question of my colleague from York East.
Adjournment Debate

The Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) had made renewal of VIAs fleet one of his top priorities. The majority of VIAs fleet is 30 years old. The equipment is expensive to operate and maintain, prone to breakdowns in severe weather conditions, and it does not offer a level of comfort and reliability which the travelling public demands from rail passenger transportation.
The Minister of Transport has asked the rail passenger action force, headed by Dr. Hugh Horner of Alberta, to make recommendations on equipment renewal as part of the mandate of the action force. The task force is to look at ways and means of bringing rail passenger services up to modern, cost-efficient standards. Specifically in terms of equipment renewal, the main option being considered is the replacement of existing rolling stock with modern, state of the art, high capacity, proven technology cars and locomotives manufactured to the highest degree possible with labour, components and engineering obtained from across Canada.
The Minister of Transport considers that new equipment is essential to the future viability of rail passenger services in Canada and, as he has previously stated, a substantial capital program of approximately $200 million exists within VIAs budget for this purpose.
Steps have already been taken to improve VIAs performance vis-a-vis service to the public, as is evidenced by a more successful Christmas season this year. Of course the essence of the Minister's objective is to strive for continued improvement in VIA Rail's performance, both financially and in the provision of rail service to the Canadian people.
